35	### A REST controller mapped to `/inventory`
36	
37	```kotlin
38	/** Controller for the inventory flow. HTTP entry point for the inventory endpoints; calls InventoryService. */
39	@RestController
40	@RequestMapping("/inventory")
41	class InventoryController (
42	    private val inventoryService: InventoryService
43	){
44	```
45	
46	**Spring (`@RestController`):** this is `@Controller` plus `@ResponseBody`, in one annotation.
47	- `@Controller` is a stereotype, so component scanning makes the class a bean (like `@Service`),
48	  and Spring MVC scans it for request mappings.
49	- `@ResponseBody` says "a function's return value **is** the response body". Spring passes it to
50	  an HTTP message converter, here Jackson, which writes it as JSON.
51	
52	With only `@Controller`, Spring would try to render an HTML **view** instead of writing the
53	body. A returned `String` is taken as the view's name. A returned object, like this list, is put
54	in the model for the view to use, and the view name comes from the URL (`inventory`). There is no
55	such template in this project, so the request fails with a `500`. That's why a JSON API uses
56	`@RestController`.
57	
58	**Spring (`@RequestMapping` on the class):** sets a base path for every handler in this class.
59	Each function's mapping is added to the end of it. Robert chose this over putting the full path on
60	each function. It's the usual Spring pattern, and it fits the next endpoint:
61	`getInventory`'s `@GetMapping("/{skuId}")` maps to `/inventory/{skuId}` ([below](#get-inventoryskuid)).
62	
63	**Kotlin:** constructor injection of the service, the same pattern as the
64	[repository](InventoryRepository.kt.md#a-spring-bean-with-constructor-injection). The space in
65	`InventoryController (` is legal and changes nothing.
66	
67	**Spring (one object, many threads):** Spring builds this controller **once, at startup**, not per
68	request. Component scanning finds the stereotypes, and Spring builds the beans bottom-up
69	(`JdbcClient` → repository → service → controller), passing each into the next constructor.
70	After that there is exactly one `InventoryController` (a *singleton*). When requests arrive,
71	Tomcat gives each one its own **thread** (up to 200 by default; the rest queue), and every thread
72	calls `listInventory()` on that **same object**. More requests means more threads, not more objects.
73	
74	That's why Spring beans must be **stateless**. A `var lastResult` field would be shared by every
75	thread: request A writes it, request B overwrites it, and A reads B's data. That's a **race
76	condition**, and it only shows up intermittently. This class only holds a `private val` reference
77	that never changes after startup, so it's safe. Purchases have the same shape of risk (read stock,
78	check, write), which is why stock changes are single atomic SQL statements.
79	
80	To see it yourself: temporarily add `println(System.identityHashCode(this))` to `listInventory()`,
81	call the endpoint twice with `bootRun` running, and see the same number both times.
82	
83	### The `// Contract:` comment
84	
85	```kotlin
86	// Contract: paths./inventory.get — 200 application/json array of InventoryItem, [] when empty.
87	```
88	
89	**Contract:** this is the file's `// Contract:` comment. It names the exact part of the API contract
90	the function below exists for, so a reviewer can jump straight to it in `inventory.yaml`:
91	`paths./inventory.get` (`operationId: listInventory`) promises a `200` with `application/json`, a
92	body that is an array of `InventoryItem`, and "If no SKUs exist, returns an empty array." The
93	comment compresses all three into one line.
94	
95	**Why this wording:** Robert's first version described the endpoint in prose ("The endpoint is a
96	simple and returns all inventory"). When the code was reviewed (2026-09-25), it was rewritten to name the contract path
97	and the rules, because a `// Contract:` comment is a pointer into the YAML, not a description.
98	
99	**Placement:** it sits above the KDoc, separated by a blank line, so the KDoc stays directly on top
100	of the function it documents.
101	
102	### `GET /inventory`
103	
104	```kotlin
105	/** Returns every SKU and its quantity for GET /inventory.*/
106	@GetMapping
107	fun listInventory(): List<InventoryItem> = inventoryService.listInventory()
108	```
109	
110	**Spring (`@GetMapping`):** short for `@RequestMapping(method = [RequestMethod.GET])`. With no
111	path of its own, it maps to the class's base path, so this function handles `GET /inventory`.
112	A `@GetMapping` also answers `HEAD` (same status and headers, no body), and Spring MVC answers
113	`OPTIONS` itself with an `Allow` header. Every other method on that path, such as `POST` or
114	`DELETE /inventory`, gets `405 Method Not Allowed`. Spring
115	matches paths exactly, and trailing-slash matching has been off by default since Spring 6, so
116	`GET /inventory/` is a `404`.
117	
118	The function's **name** doesn't matter to Spring. Only the annotation does. `listInventory`,
119	`list` or `getInventory` would all be routed the same way. Robert first called it
120	`findAllInventory` and renamed it to `listInventory` in review, to match the contract's
121	`operationId: listInventory` and the service function. One name then runs from the YAML through
122	the controller to the service, which makes the code easy to trace. The tests call the endpoint by
123	its URL through MockMvc (a simulated HTTP request), never the function by name, so the rename didn't
124	touch them.
125	
126	**KDoc style:** the KDoc starts with a verb and says what the function does ("Returns every SKU…"),
127	not what kind of thing it is ("A function that…"). The signature already shows it's a function.
128	
129	**Spring (what happens after `return`):**
130	1. The `DispatcherServlet` receives the request and finds this function through its mapping.
131	2. The function returns a `List<InventoryItem>`.
132	3. Because of `@ResponseBody`, Spring picks a message converter that can write a list for the
133	   client's `Accept` header (MockMvc sends none, which means "anything"). Jackson's JSON
134	   converter matches, so the response gets `Content-Type: application/json`.
135	4. Jackson writes the list as a JSON array, one object per item, with the Kotlin property
136	   names as keys ([see InventoryItem](InventoryItem.kt.md)). An empty list becomes `[]`.
137	
138	The status is `200 OK` because nothing threw and nothing set another status. If the database
139	fails, the exception passes through here untouched, and Spring Boot's error handling answers `500`
140	(see [why the service has no try/catch](InventoryService.kt.md#listinventory)).
141	
142	**Kotlin:** an [expression body](../../test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md#the-container-bean)
143	again. The return type is written out, even though Kotlin could infer it from `listInventory()`.
144	On a public function that's the better choice: the signature shows what the endpoint returns
145	without anyone having to look at the service.
146	
147	**Contract:** returning `List<InventoryItem>` is what makes the body "an array of `InventoryItem`".
148	The empty-array rule comes from the repository returning an empty list, and the SKU order from its
149	`ORDER BY sku_id`, not from anything here. The controller never sorts or filters.
150	`InventoryControllerTest` checks both cases with `JsonCompareMode.STRICT`.
151	
152	### The second `// Contract:` comment
153	
154	```kotlin
155	// Contract: paths./inventory/{skuId}.get - 200 application/json with InventoryItem, 404 with text/plain when SkuNotFoundException is thrown.
156	```
157	
158	**Contract:** `paths./inventory/{skuId}.get` (`operationId: getInventory`) promises a `200` with an
159	`InventoryItem` as JSON, and a `404` whose body is the `Error` schema (a plain string) as
160	`text/plain` when "the SKU does not exist". The comment names both, and names the exception that
161	triggers the `404`, because nothing in this file produces it. A reader following the `404` needs
162	to know to look for `SkuNotFoundException`, which leads to the handler.
163	
164	### `GET /inventory/{skuId}`
165	
166	```kotlin
167	/** Returns an SKU and its quantity for GET /inventory/{skuId}. */
168	@GetMapping("/{skuId}")
169	fun getInventory(@PathVariable skuId: String): InventoryItem = inventoryService.getInventory(skuId)
170	```
171	
172	**Spring (path templates):** `"/{skuId}"` is appended to the class's `/inventory`, giving
173	`/inventory/{skuId}`. The braces mark a **path variable**: that segment matches any text up to the
174	next `/`. So `/inventory/widget` matches with `skuId = "widget"`. `/inventory/widget/purchase` doesn't
175	match this mapping (it has one segment too many); that path will get its own mapping later.
176	`/inventory` alone still goes to `listInventory`, because it has no segment for `{skuId}`.
177	
178	**Spring (`@PathVariable`):** tells Spring to fill this parameter from the path variable. With no
179	name given, it uses the **parameter's name**, so the Kotlin name `skuId` must match `{skuId}`
180	exactly. Spring can read Kotlin parameter names at runtime (the Spring Boot Gradle plugin turns on the
181	compiler's `javaParameters` option, and Spring can also read Kotlin's own metadata). If the names differed, you'd
182	write `@PathVariable("skuId") id: String`. Spring also URL-decodes the segment first, so a request
183	for `/inventory/caf%C3%A9` arrives as `café`.
184	
185	**When a name mismatch fails** (walkthrough, 2026-09-28): `@GetMapping("/{skuId}")` with
186	`@PathVariable sku: String` compiles, because `"/{skuId}"` is just a string to the compiler, and the
187	app starts, because Spring doesn't compare placeholders with parameters when it registers the mapping.
188	It fails on the first request: Spring throws `MissingPathVariableException` and answers `500`, since
189	it's a server bug, not a client mistake. Only a test that sends a real request through MockMvc
190	catches it; calling `controller.getInventory("widget")` directly would skip path matching and pass.
191	
192	**Kotlin (annotating a parameter):** an annotation can sit directly in front of a parameter,
193	inside the parentheses, the same as in Java.
194	
195	**Kotlin + Spring (non-null `String`):** the parameter is `String`, not `String?`. A path variable is
196	always present when the mapping matches, so it can't be null, and the type says so. (A `String?`
197	parameter would tell Spring the value is optional.)
198	
199	**Spring (the exception path):** when the service throws `SkuNotFoundException`, the exception passes
200	straight out of this function. Nothing is caught here. Spring's `DispatcherServlet` catches it,
201	asks its exception resolvers whether anyone handles that type, and finds
202	[`InventoryExceptionHandler.handleSkuNotFound`](error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt.md). Its
203	`ResponseEntity` becomes the response. Before the handler existed, nothing matched, so the exception
204	went up to the servlet container as a `500`. MockMvc has no container, so the tests saw it as a
205	`ServletException`.
206	
207	**Why the function stays a one-liner:** Robert chose `@RestControllerAdvice` over building a
208	`ResponseEntity` here (2026-09-27). The controller keeps the happy path (return an `InventoryItem`,
209	Spring writes `200` JSON), and error mapping lives in one place for every endpoint. The rejected
210	version would have been an `if`/`?:` in this function that built a `404` `ResponseEntity`, with the
211	return type changed to `ResponseEntity<*>`. It can't be `ResponseEntity<InventoryItem>`, because
212	the error body is a `String`, not an `InventoryItem`, so the type would stop saying what the
213	endpoint returns.
214	
215	**Naming:** `getInventory` matches the contract's `operationId: getInventory` and the service
216	function, the same one-name rule as `listInventory`. Kotlin allows it even though the class also has
217	a `listInventory`: the names differ. Overloading (two functions with the *same* name and different
218	parameters) would also be allowed, as in Java.
219	
220	**Contract:** returning `InventoryItem` gives the `200` body `{"skuId": ..., "quantity": ...}`. A
221	sold-out SKU is still a row, so it comes back as `200` with `"quantity": 0`, never `404`
222	(`InventoryControllerTest` checks this).
223	
224	### The third `// Contract:` comment
225	
226	```kotlin
227	// Contract: paths./inventory/{skuId}.post - 200 application/json with InventoryItem, 400 text/plain for a quantity below 1, an unreadable body, the wrong Content-Type, or an add that would overflow.
228	```
229	
230	**Contract:** `paths./inventory/{skuId}.post` (`operationId: createInventory`) lists two
231	responses: `200` with an `InventoryItem` as JSON ("the updated inventory state for the SKU"), and
232	`400` "Invalid request" as `text/plain`. The contract doesn't say *which* requests are invalid; the
233	four cases here are the README's "Contract gaps (POST)" decisions. Like the `404` comment above,
234	it names cases this file never handles itself, so a reader knows to look in the exception handler.
235	Robert's first version listed only the overflow case.
236	
237	### `POST /inventory/{skuId}`
238	
239	```kotlin
240	/** Adds quantity to the SKU's stock, creating the SKU if it's new, and returns the new total for POST /inventory/{skuId}.*/
241	@PostMapping("/{skuId}")
242	fun receiveInventory(@PathVariable skuId: String, @Valid @RequestBody requestQuantity: InventoryQuantity): InventoryItem = inventoryService.receiveInventory(skuId, requestQuantity.quantity)
243	```
244	
245	**Spring (`@PostMapping`):** the `POST` version of [`@GetMapping`](#get-inventory), with the same
246	path template as `getInventory`. `GET` and `POST` to `/inventory/{skuId}` are two different
247	mappings, and Spring picks one by the HTTP method. `@PathVariable` works exactly as in
248	[`getInventory`](#get-inventoryskuid).
249	
250	**Spring (`@RequestBody`):** fills this parameter from the request **body**. Spring picks a message
251	converter by the request's `Content-Type`: for `application/json` that's Jackson, which builds an
252	`InventoryQuantity` through its primary constructor (see
253	[InventoryQuantity](InventoryQuantity.kt.md#the-class)). It's the reverse of what
254	[`@ResponseBody`](#a-rest-controller-mapped-to-inventory) does with the return value.
255	`@RequestBody` is `required = true` by default, so a missing or `null` body is an error, matching
256	the contract's `requestBody: required: true`.
257	
258	Unlike `@PathVariable`, the parameter **name** doesn't matter here: there's only one body, so
259	`requestQuantity` could be called anything. The JSON field names are matched against
260	`InventoryQuantity`'s properties, not against this parameter.
261	
262	**Spring (`@Valid`):** tells Spring to run Bean Validation on the object after Jackson builds it.
263	That's what makes `@Min(1)` on `quantity` do anything. Without `@Valid`, `{"quantity": 0}` would
264	reach the service. (The service's own [`require`](InventoryService.kt.md#receiveinventory-a-precondition-and-a-block-body)
265	would then stop it, but as a `500`, not the contract's `400`.) The order of `@Valid` and
266	`@RequestBody` doesn't matter.
267	
268	**Spring (what happens before this function runs):** the function body only runs if all of this
269	succeeds. Each step that fails throws an exception, and the function is never called:
270	
271	| Step | Fails when | Exception | Handler's response |
272	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
273	| 1. Find a converter for the `Content-Type` | not JSON, e.g. `text/plain` | `HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException` | `400 Content-Type must be application/json` |
274	| 2. Jackson reads the body into `InventoryQuantity` | empty, malformed, wrong type, too big, `null` | `HttpMessageNotReadableException` | `400 Invalid request body` |
275	| 3. `@Valid` runs Bean Validation | `quantity < 1` | `MethodArgumentNotValidException` | `400 quantity must be at least 1` |
276	| 4. The function calls the service | the total would overflow | `AddStockOverflowException` | `400 Quantity would exceed the maximum stock` |
277	
278	Steps 1 to 3 are Spring's own exceptions. Without handlers, Spring's built-in resolver answers them
279	(`415` for step 1, a `400` for steps 2 and 3, with Spring Boot's JSON error body in the running app
280	and an empty body under MockMvc, never the contract's `text/plain` string); the
281	[exception handler](error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt.md) overrides that to match the contract.
282	
283	**Why the service gets `requestQuantity.quantity`, not the object:** the request body is an HTTP
284	shape. The service takes plain `String` + `Int` and never depends on a web class (see the
285	[service notes](InventoryService.kt.md#receiveinventory-a-precondition-and-a-block-body)). Robert's
286	first version passed a bare `quantity`, which doesn't exist in this scope: the `Int` is inside
287	the object, so it has to be read with `.quantity`.
288	
289	**Why `200` and not `201 Created`:** a `POST` that creates something is often a `201`. The contract
290	lists only `200`, for both "created" and "added to", and the tests check it. Returning
291	`InventoryItem` (not a `ResponseEntity`) gives Spring's default `200`.
292	
293	**Where is the 200 enforced?** (walkthrough, 2026-09-29) Nowhere in production code: it's a
294	default. Getting `201` would take `@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)` on the function, or a
295	`ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED)` return. What pins the `200` is the test:
296	`status { isOk() }` in `InventoryControllerTest`'s `POST inventory creates a new SKU`. Defaults
297	don't show up in code, so a test has to pin them.
298	
299	**Naming:** `receiveInventory` matches the service function, the "one name through the layers" rule.
300	It does *not* match the contract's `operationId: createInventory`: this endpoint creates **or**
301	adds, and "receive" (from the brief's "receiving new stock") covers both. Robert's first name,
302	`postInventory`, described the HTTP verb rather than the action, and shared its name with the test
303	helper, which made the tests confusing to read.
304	
305	**Kotlin:** an expression body again, with a missing `:` before the return type in Robert's first
306	version (`fun f(...) InventoryItem = ...` doesn't compile).
307	
308	**Contract:** the body is an `InventoryItem`: `RETURNING` in the repository gives the row as it is
309	after the change, so the response is the new total. `InventoryControllerTest` checks both a new
310	SKU (`10`) and an existing one (`5 + 3 = 8`) with `JsonCompareMode.STRICT`.

325	# InventoryExceptionHandler.kt
326	
327	> Source: [src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt](../../../../../../src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-28
328	
329	## Role
330	
331	Written by Robert. It turns exceptions into HTTP error responses. It sits *beside* the request flow,
332	not in it. It handles five exceptions of two kinds: ours, thrown by the service, and Spring's own,
333	thrown while Spring reads the request, before the controller function runs. Without this class,
334	ours would become `500`s and Spring's would get Spring's default `400` or `415`, never the
335	contract's `text/plain` text.
336	
337	| Exception | From | Response |
338	| --- | --- | --- |
339	| [`SkuNotFoundException`](SkuNotFoundException.kt.md) | our service | `404` `SKU not found: <skuId>` |
340	| [`AddStockOverflowException`](AddStockOverflowException.kt.md) | our service | `400` `Quantity would exceed the maximum stock` |
341	| `MethodArgumentNotValidException` | Spring (Bean Validation) | `400` with the `@Min` message |
342	| `HttpMessageNotReadableException` | Spring (Jackson) | `400` `Invalid request body` |
343	| `HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException` | Spring (content negotiation) | `400` `Content-Type must be application/json` |
344	
345	Every body is `text/plain`. The purchase endpoint will add its own handlers here, so every error body
346	the contract requires is built in one file.
347	
348	## Walkthrough
349	
350	### Imports
351	
352	```kotlin
353	import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus
354	import org.springframework.http.MediaType
355	import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity
356	import org.springframework.http.converter.HttpMessageNotReadableException
357	import org.springframework.web.HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException
358	import org.springframework.web.bind.MethodArgumentNotValidException
359	import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.ExceptionHandler
360	import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestControllerAdvice
361	```
362	
363	**Kotlin:** `SkuNotFoundException` and `AddStockOverflowException` are in the same package
364	(`inventory.error`), so they need no import. The three Spring exceptions do. Robert's first
365	`MethodArgumentNotValidException` handler didn't compile for exactly this reason: his own exceptions
366	had never needed an import, so the rule hadn't come up.
367	`org.springframework.http` holds the HTTP building blocks (status codes, media types, responses);
368	`web.bind.annotation` holds the Spring MVC annotations, the same package as `@GetMapping`. Note
369	`web.bind` (the exception) vs `web.bind.annotation` (the annotations): two different packages.
370	
371	### The class, and why it's an advice
372	
373	```kotlin
374	// Why: RestController advice so spring will catch and return specific responses we have built out for every controller rather than us building out multiple response entities for each controller. We rejected ResponseStatusException because its body is JSON, not text/plain.
375	
376	/** Where the various custom built exceptions and spring exceptions are transformed to HTTP responses. */
377	@RestControllerAdvice
378	class InventoryExceptionHandler{
379	```
380	
381	**Spring (`@RestControllerAdvice`):** it's `@ControllerAdvice` plus `@ResponseBody`, the same pairing
382	as [`@RestController`](../InventoryController.kt.md#a-rest-controller-mapped-to-inventory).
383	- `@ControllerAdvice` is a stereotype (it's annotated with `@Component`), so component scanning makes
384	  this class a bean at startup. Spring MVC then remembers it as a source of `@ExceptionHandler`
385	  methods that apply to **every** controller.
386	- `@ResponseBody` means a handler's return value is written as the response body. Here the return
387	  type is `ResponseEntity`, which is always written as the response anyway, so this half isn't
388	  strictly needed. It would matter for a handler that returned a plain `String`.
389	
390	Think of it as one `try`/`catch` that Spring wraps around every controller method, written once
391	instead of in each controller.
392	
393	**Why:** the `// Why:` records Robert's decision (2026-09-27). The two rejected options:
394	- **A `ResponseEntity` built in the controller.** The controller would need an `if`/`?:` and a
395	  `ResponseEntity<*>` return type, and every endpoint that can miss a SKU (purchase too) would repeat
396	  it. With the advice, controllers keep the happy path only.
397	- **`ResponseStatusException`.** The service would throw an exception that carries an HTTP status,
398	  so HTTP knowledge would leak into the service layer. That's the stronger reason. The body is
399	  also wrong by default: Spring Boot renders it through its error page, which means JSON for API
400	  clients, an HTML page for browsers, and an empty body under MockMvc (no error page there). None
401	  of these is the contract's `text/plain` string. (An advice *could* catch `ResponseStatusException`
402	  and write text itself, but then the custom exception is simpler.) The `// Why:` comment's "its body is
403	  JSON" is the common case, not the whole story.
404	
405	**Placement:** the `// Why:` sits above the KDoc, with a blank line between, so the KDoc stays
406	directly on the class. Robert's first version put the comment between the KDoc and
407	`@RestControllerAdvice`. That cuts the KDoc off from the class: it no longer shows on hover, and
408	`check_kdoc.py` flagged the class as undocumented.
409	
410	**Kotlin:** no constructor parameters, because the handler needs nothing injected. A class with no
411	primary constructor parameters is declared with just its name, as here. Spring calls its no-argument
412	constructor. `InventoryExceptionHandler{` with no space is legal.
413	
414	### The `// Contract:` comment
415	
416	```kotlin
417	// Contract: paths./inventory/{skuId}.get - 404 with text/plain when SkuNotFoundException is thrown.
418	```
419	
420	**Contract:** `paths./inventory/{skuId}.get`, response `'404'`: content `text/plain`, schema
421	`#/components/schemas/Error` (`type: string`). This comment is the other end of the one in the
422	[controller](../InventoryController.kt.md#the-second--contract-comment): the controller says the `404`
423	comes from `SkuNotFoundException`, and this file is where it's produced.
424	
425	### `handleSkuNotFound`
426	
427	```kotlin
428	/** Returns a 404 text/plain response whose body is the exception's message. */
429	@ExceptionHandler(SkuNotFoundException::class)
430	fun handleSkuNotFound(ex: SkuNotFoundException ): ResponseEntity<String> =
431	
432	    ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
433	        .contentType(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
434	        .body(ex.message ?: "SKU not found.")
435	```
436	
437	**Spring (`@ExceptionHandler`):** registers this function for `SkuNotFoundException` (and any
438	subclass of it). When a controller method throws, Spring's `DispatcherServlet` asks its exception
439	resolvers for a match, in this order:
440	1. an `@ExceptionHandler` inside the controller class itself,
441	2. then `@ExceptionHandler`s in `@ControllerAdvice` beans, like this one,
442	3. then `@ResponseStatus` on the exception class and `ResponseStatusException`,
443	4. then Spring's built-in mappings (e.g. a malformed request → `400`),
444	5. and if nothing matches, a `500` with Spring Boot's default JSON error body.
445	
446	Spring catches *every* exception, custom or not: the advice isn't where Spring looks when it
447	"doesn't recognize" an exception (the 2026-09-28 walkthrough's first framing). It just gets a
448	custom exception handled at step 2 instead of falling through to the `500` at step 5.
449	
450	Within one class, if several handlers match, the one for the *closest* exception type wins, so a
451	later `@ExceptionHandler(RuntimeException::class)` in this class wouldn't steal this one's
452	exceptions. Across several advice classes, their order (`@Order`) decides first: the first advice
453	with *any* matching handler wins. Spring passes the thrown exception in as the
454	parameter, and the function's return value becomes the response.
455	
456	`SkuNotFoundException::class` is a [class reference](../../../test/InventoryApplicationTests.kt.md#starting-the-real-application-in-a-test),
457	Kotlin's `SkuNotFoundException.class`.
458	
459	**Spring (`ResponseEntity` builder):** `ResponseEntity` is a whole HTTP response: status, headers and
460	body. It's built with a chain where each call returns a builder, and the last call produces the
461	response:
462	
463	| Call | Sets | Returns |
464	| --- | --- | --- |
465	| `ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)` | status `404` | a `BodyBuilder` |
466	| `.contentType(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)` | the `Content-Type` header | the same `BodyBuilder` |
467	| `.body(...)` | the body | `ResponseEntity<String>` |
468	
469	The body's type becomes the `T` in `ResponseEntity<T>`, which is why the return type is
470	`ResponseEntity<String>`. Spring then writes the `String` as-is with its `StringHttpMessageConverter`
471	(no JSON quotes around it).
472	
473	Two things this chain avoids:
474	- **`ResponseEntity.notFound()`** looks like a shortcut, but it returns a `HeadersBuilder`, which has
475	  no `.body(...)`. Only `.build()`, giving an empty `404`.
476	- **Leaving out `.contentType(...)`.** Spring would then choose the type from the request's
477	  `Accept` header, and could send `application/json` for a client that asks for JSON. Setting it
478	  here makes the `text/plain` promise hold for every client.
479	
480	Robert's first version used `HttpStatus.CONFLICT` (409), copied from a parallel example. Both
481	`404` tests caught it: `Status expected:<404> but was:<409>`.
482	
483	**Kotlin (`message` is nullable):** `ex.message` comes from Java's `Throwable.getMessage()`, which
484	may return null, so Kotlin types it `String?`. `body(...)` here needs a `String`, so the null case
485	must be handled. The [Elvis operator](../InventoryService.kt.md#getinventory-turning-no-row-into-an-error)
486	gives a fallback. The three options that were weighed:
487	
488	| Option | If `message` were null | Chosen? |
489	| --- | --- | --- |
490	| `ex.message ?: "SKU not found."` | a readable fallback body | **yes** |
491	| `ex.message!!` | throws a `NullPointerException` inside the error handler | no |
492	| keep `skuId` as a `val` on the exception and build the text here | can't be null | no |
493	
494	In practice the fallback never runs: `SkuNotFoundException`'s constructor always passes
495	`"SKU not found: $skuId"`, so `message` is never null. The `?:` is there because the compiler can't
496	see that. Robert chose a readable fallback over an empty string (2026-09-27), because a client
497	getting an empty `404` body would have nothing to go on.
498	
499	**Worth knowing: handled exceptions aren't logged.** Once this handler returns, Spring treats the
500	exception as dealt with and logs nothing at the default log level. The fallback text only ever
501	reaches the API client. If missing SKUs should show up in the logs, that's a logger call in this
502	function.
503	
504	**Worth knowing: no charset in the header.** Checked against the running app on 2026-09-27:
505	`curl -i http://localhost:8080/inventory/missing` returns `Content-Type: text/plain`, with no
506	`charset` parameter, while the body bytes are UTF-8 (a SKU `café` comes back as UTF-8 bytes). For
507	ASCII SKUs this makes no difference. A client that assumes a different charset could misread
508	non-ASCII ones. `MediaType("text", "plain", Charsets.UTF_8)` would state it; this is tracked in TODO.
509	
510	**Kotlin:** an [expression body](../../../test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md#the-container-bean)
511	split across lines. The blank line after `=` is legal, and each line starting with `.` continues the
512	chain. The space in `SkuNotFoundException )` changes nothing.
513	
514	**Naming:** `handle` + what went wrong is the usual Spring convention, so each function name says
515	which case it covers. Robert first reused the class name, `inventoryExceptionHandler`, and renamed
516	it in review.
517	
518	**Contract:** status `404`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, and a body that is a bare string: the `Error`
519	schema is `type: string`, not an object. `InventoryControllerTest` checks all three, with
520	`contentTypeCompatibleWith(TEXT_PLAIN)` so a later `;charset=UTF-8` would still pass.
521	
522	### `handleStockOverflow`: our exception, our message
523	
524	```kotlin
525	// Contract: paths./inventory/{skuId}.post - 400 with text/plain when AddStockOverflowException is thrown.
526	
527	/** Returns a 400 text/plain response whose body is the exception's message.*/
528	@ExceptionHandler(AddStockOverflowException::class)
529	fun handleStockOverflow(ex: AddStockOverflowException): ResponseEntity<String> =
530	
531	    ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST)
532	        .contentType(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
533	        .body(ex.message ?: "Overflow Guard Triggered")
534	```
535	
536	**Spring:** the same shape as `handleSkuNotFound`, with `HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST` (`400`) instead of
537	`NOT_FOUND`. Robert's first version kept `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` from an earlier draft; the overflow
538	test caught it (`Status expected:<400> but was:<500>`). Each `HttpStatus` constant is just a name
539	for a number, and the client gets whatever is passed to `status(...)`.
540	
541	**Why `ex.message` is safe here:** we wrote this exception's message for the client
542	(`"Quantity would exceed the maximum stock"`, in
543	[AddStockOverflowException](AddStockOverflowException.kt.md)). As with `SkuNotFoundException`, the
544	`?:` fallback never runs; it's only there because `Throwable.message` is typed `String?`.
545	
546	**Contract:** `paths./inventory/{skuId}.post`, response `'400'`, `text/plain`. The overflow case
547	itself is a README "Contract gaps (POST)" decision.
548	
549	### `handleValidationFailure`: the message from `@Min`
550	
551	```kotlin
552	// Contract: paths./inventory/{skuId}.post - a request body that fails validation is a 400 text/plain.
553	
554	/** Returns a 400 text/plain response from the failing field's validation message.*/
555	@ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException::class)
556	fun handleValidationFailure(ex: MethodArgumentNotValidException): ResponseEntity<String> =
557	
558	    ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST)
559	        .contentType(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
560	        .body(ex.bindingResult.fieldError?.defaultMessage ?: "Invalid request")
561	```
562	
563	**Spring (handling Spring's own exceptions):** `MethodArgumentNotValidException` is what
564	`@Valid @RequestBody` throws when Bean Validation fails. An advice doesn't care whose exception it
565	handles. Because `@ExceptionHandler` methods in advice are tried (step 2 in the list above) before
566	Spring's built-in mappings (step 4), this handler replaces Spring's default answer: a `400` without
567	our text (Spring Boot's JSON error body in the running app, an empty body under MockMvc).
568	
569	**Why not `ex.message`:** for Spring's exceptions the message is written for developers, not
570	clients. Robert's first version returned it, and the test showed what the client would have got:
571	
572	```text
573	Validation failed for argument [1] in public com.robertwoolbright.inventory.inventory.InventoryItem
574	com.robertwoolbright.inventory.inventory.InventoryController.receiveInventory(java.lang.String,...
575	```
576	
577	That leaks the package, class and method names to anyone calling the API. The `?:` fallback didn't
578	help either: `?:` only runs when the left side is `null`, and Spring's messages never are.
579	
580	**Kotlin (a chain of safe calls):** the message the client should see is the one in
581	`@Min(message = ...)`. Spring stores it on the exception:
582	
583	| Expression | Type | What it is |
584	| --- | --- | --- |
585	| `ex.bindingResult` | `BindingResult` | every validation error for the body |
586	| `.fieldError` | `FieldError?` | the first error on a field; `null` if none |
587	| `?.defaultMessage` | `String?` | that error's message, here `"quantity must be at least 1"` |
588	| `?: "Invalid request"` | `String` | the fallback if anything above was `null` |
589	
590	`?.` is the **safe-call operator**: `a?.b` is `a.b` if `a` isn't `null`, and `null` if it is, instead
591	of a `NullPointerException`. One `?:` at the end covers a `null` from any step in the chain. Java
592	equivalent:
593	
594	```java
595	FieldError error = ex.getBindingResult().getFieldError();
596	String message = (error != null && error.getDefaultMessage() != null)
597	        ? error.getDefaultMessage() : "Invalid request";
598	```
599	
600	Both `fieldError` and `defaultMessage` are Java getters marked `@Nullable` in Spring, so Kotlin
601	types them `T?` and the compiler insists on `?.` (see [platform types](../../../build.gradle.kts.md#compiler-options)).
602	
603	**Why read it from the exception, not hardcode it:** Robert's second version returned the fixed text
604	`"quantity must be at least 1"`. The tests passed, but the text then lived in two places, and the
605	handler would say "quantity must be at least 1" for *any* validation failure, including rules added
606	later. Reading `defaultMessage` keeps the annotation as the single source of the text.
607	
608	**Only the first error:** `fieldError` returns one error. The request body has one field today, so
609	there's only ever one. With several fields, the client would see the first failure only.
610	
611	**Naming:** first `handleMalformedBody` (wrong: a malformed body is the next handler's job), then
612	`handleMinQuantity`, renamed in review to `handleValidationFailure`, because the advice is global
613	and will catch every Bean Validation failure on any `@Valid` body, not just `@Min`. The fallback and
614	KDoc were made general at the same time. Spring never calls the method by name, so the rename
615	couldn't change behavior.
616	
617	### `handleInvalidRequestBody`: a handler with no parameters
618	
619	```kotlin
620	// Contract: paths./inventory/{skuId}.post - when the request body is invalid we return a 400 text/plain.
621	
622	/** Returns a 400 text/plain response with the fixed text Invalid request body.*/
623	@ExceptionHandler(HttpMessageNotReadableException::class)
624	fun handleInvalidRequestBody(): ResponseEntity<String> =
625	
626	    ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST)
627	        .contentType(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
628	        .body("Invalid request body")
629	```
630	
631	**Spring:** `HttpMessageNotReadableException` covers every way reading the body can fail: empty,
632	malformed JSON, `null`, an array, a missing or `null` `quantity`, a string, a decimal, or a number too
633	big for `Int` (the nine cases in
634	[InventoryControllerTest](../../../test/inventory/InventoryControllerTest.kt.md#every-unreadable-body-is-a-400)).
635	They all get the same fixed text, the README "Contract gaps (POST)" decision.
636	
637	**Why a fixed string:** the exception's message is Jackson's, for example
638	`JSON parse error: Cannot coerce String value ("5") to 'int' value (but might if coercion using 'CoercionConfig' was enabled)`.
639	It names internal settings and differs for every case. There's nothing useful in it for the client
640	that "Invalid request body" doesn't say.
641	
642	**Spring (no parameters):** once the body doesn't need the exception, the parameter can go. The
643	exception type in `@ExceptionHandler(...)` is what routes the exception here; the parameter is only
644	there when you want to *read* it. Spring looks at the parameter list, finds nothing to fill in, and
645	calls the function with no arguments. With the parameter gone, the signature itself shows which
646	handlers use the exception and which don't. Robert's first try removed only the name, leaving
647	`(HttpMessageNotReadableException)`. Kotlin reads that as a parameter *named*
648	`HttpMessageNotReadableException` with no type: "An explicit type is required on a value parameter".
649	A parameter is always `name: Type`, in Java too.
650	
651	### `handleContentTypeMismatch`: 400 instead of Spring's 415
652	
653	```kotlin
654	// Contract: paths./inventory/{skuId}.post - when the content type is not application/json we return a 400 text/plain.
655	
656	/** Returns a 400 text/plain response with the fixed text Content-Type must be application/json.*/
657	@ExceptionHandler(HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException::class)
658	fun handleContentTypeMismatch():ResponseEntity<String> =
659	
660	    ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST)
661	        .contentType(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
662	        .body("Content-Type must be application/json")
663	```
664	
665	**Spring:** `@RequestBody` throws `HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException` when no message converter can
666	read the request's `Content-Type` into `InventoryQuantity` (only Jackson can, and only for JSON).
667	Spring's default answer is `415 Unsupported Media Type`: correct HTTP, but the contract lists only
668	`200` and `400`. This handler overrides it.
669	
670	Robert's first version returned `HttpStatus.UNSUPPORTED_MEDIA_TYPE` here, so the handler *was*
671	running but sent `415` on purpose. The status comes from the code, not from the exception.
672	
673	**Why:** a `415` is arguably the better HTTP answer, but a client written against the contract
674	only expects `200` or `400`. Sticking to the contract was the README decision (2026-09-28).
675	
676	**Spring (global reach):** like every handler here, this one applies to every controller. Any future
677	endpoint with a `@RequestBody` gets the same `400` for a non-JSON request, which is what we want.
678	
679	**Kotlin:** `():ResponseEntity<String>` with no spaces is legal. Robert's first version also copied
680	the body from the handler above (`"Invalid request body"`); the test caught the wrong text.
681	
682	## Check your understanding
683	
684	- Remove `@RestControllerAdvice` and run `GET /inventory/missing`. What status comes back, and why
685	  does the handler function no longer run?
686	- A second handler, `@ExceptionHandler(RuntimeException::class)`, is added to this class. Which
687	  handler answers a missing SKU, and which answers a database failure?
688	- What would the client receive with `ResponseEntity.notFound().build()` instead of the chain?
689	- Why does `ex.message` need `?:` even though the message can never be null here?
690	- `handleInvalidRequestBody` returned `ex.message ?: "Invalid request body"`. What would the client see for `{"quantity": "5"}`, and why does the fallback never appear?
691	- Delete `handleContentTypeMismatch`. What does a `text/plain` POST get now, and which part of Spring produces it?
692	- What does `ex.bindingResult.fieldError?.defaultMessage` evaluate to for `{"quantity": 0}`? When would the `?:` fallback be used?
693	- Why is `ex.message` fine to send for `AddStockOverflowException` but not for `HttpMessageNotReadableException`?

# InventoryController.kt

> Source: [src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryController.kt](../../../../../src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryController.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-29

## Role

The web layer, written by Robert, and the top of the request flow: **controller** → service →
repository. It turns HTTP requests for `GET /inventory`, `GET /inventory/{skuId}` and
`POST /inventory/{skuId}` into calls to the [service](InventoryService.kt.md), and hands the result
back to Spring to write as JSON. It holds no logic of its own. Not even the `404` or the `400`s:
those come from [`InventoryExceptionHandler`](error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt.md).
[InventoryControllerTest](../../test/inventory/InventoryControllerTest.kt.md) checks it end to end
through MockMvc.

## Walkthrough

### Imports

```kotlin
import jakarta.validation.Valid
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PathVariable
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PostMapping
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestBody
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestMapping
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController
```

**Spring:** the mapping annotations come from Spring MVC's `web.bind.annotation` package, which is
on the classpath through `spring-boot-starter-webmvc` (see [build.gradle.kts](../../build.gradle.kts.md)).
`@Valid` is different: it's from Bean Validation (`jakarta.validation`), through
`spring-boot-starter-validation`, the same library as `@Min` in
[InventoryQuantity](InventoryQuantity.kt.md#the-import).

### A REST controller mapped to `/inventory`

```kotlin
/** Controller for the inventory flow. HTTP entry point for the inventory endpoints; calls InventoryService. */
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/inventory")
class InventoryController (
    private val inventoryService: InventoryService
){
```

**Spring (`@RestController`):** this is `@Controller` plus `@ResponseBody`, in one annotation.
- `@Controller` is a stereotype, so component scanning makes the class a bean (like `@Service`),
  and Spring MVC scans it for request mappings.
- `@ResponseBody` says "a function's return value **is** the response body". Spring passes it to
  an HTTP message converter, here Jackson, which writes it as JSON.

With only `@Controller`, Spring would try to render an HTML **view** instead of writing the
body. A returned `String` is taken as the view's name. A returned object, like this list, is put
in the model for the view to use, and the view name comes from the URL (`inventory`). There is no
such template in this project, so the request fails with a `500`. That's why a JSON API uses
`@RestController`.

**Spring (`@RequestMapping` on the class):** sets a base path for every handler in this class.
Each function's mapping is added to the end of it. Robert chose this over putting the full path on
each function. It's the usual Spring pattern, and it fits the next endpoint:
`getInventory`'s `@GetMapping("/{skuId}")` maps to `/inventory/{skuId}` ([below](#get-inventoryskuid)).

**Kotlin:** constructor injection of the service, the same pattern as the
[repository](InventoryRepository.kt.md#a-spring-bean-with-constructor-injection). The space in
`InventoryController (` is legal and changes nothing.

**Spring (one object, many threads):** Spring builds this controller **once, at startup**, not per
request. Component scanning finds the stereotypes, and Spring builds the beans bottom-up
(`JdbcClient` → repository → service → controller), passing each into the next constructor.
After that there is exactly one `InventoryController` (a *singleton*). When requests arrive,
Tomcat gives each one its own **thread** (up to 200 by default; the rest queue), and every thread
calls `listInventory()` on that **same object**. More requests means more threads, not more objects.

That's why Spring beans must be **stateless**. A `var lastResult` field would be shared by every
thread: request A writes it, request B overwrites it, and A reads B's data. That's a **race
condition**, and it only shows up intermittently. This class only holds a `private val` reference
that never changes after startup, so it's safe. Purchases have the same shape of risk (read stock,
check, write), which is why stock changes are single atomic SQL statements.

To see it yourself: temporarily add `println(System.identityHashCode(this))` to `listInventory()`,
call the endpoint twice with `bootRun` running, and see the same number both times.

### The `// Contract:` comment

```kotlin
// Contract: paths./inventory.get — 200 application/json array of InventoryItem, [] when empty.
```

**Contract:** this is the file's `// Contract:` comment. It names the exact part of the API contract
the function below exists for, so a reviewer can jump straight to it in `inventory.yaml`:
`paths./inventory.get` (`operationId: listInventory`) promises a `200` with `application/json`, a
body that is an array of `InventoryItem`, and "If no SKUs exist, returns an empty array." The
comment compresses all three into one line.

**Why this wording:** Robert's first version described the endpoint in prose ("The endpoint is a
simple and returns all inventory"). When the code was reviewed (2026-09-25), it was rewritten to name the contract path
and the rules, because a `// Contract:` comment is a pointer into the YAML, not a description.

**Placement:** it sits above the KDoc, separated by a blank line, so the KDoc stays directly on top
of the function it documents.

### `GET /inventory`

```kotlin
/** Returns every SKU and its quantity for GET /inventory.*/
@GetMapping
fun listInventory(): List<InventoryItem> = inventoryService.listInventory()
```

**Spring (`@GetMapping`):** short for `@RequestMapping(method = [RequestMethod.GET])`. With no
path of its own, it maps to the class's base path, so this function handles `GET /inventory`.
A `@GetMapping` also answers `HEAD` (same status and headers, no body), and Spring MVC answers
`OPTIONS` itself with an `Allow` header. Every other method on that path, such as `POST` or
`DELETE /inventory`, gets `405 Method Not Allowed`. Spring
matches paths exactly, and trailing-slash matching has been off by default since Spring 6, so
`GET /inventory/` is a `404`.

The function's **name** doesn't matter to Spring. Only the annotation does. `listInventory`,
`list` or `getInventory` would all be routed the same way. Robert first called it
`findAllInventory` and renamed it to `listInventory` in review, to match the contract's
`operationId: listInventory` and the service function. One name then runs from the YAML through
the controller to the service, which makes the code easy to trace. The tests call the endpoint by
its URL through MockMvc (a simulated HTTP request), never the function by name, so the rename didn't
touch them.

**KDoc style:** the KDoc starts with a verb and says what the function does ("Returns every SKU…"),
not what kind of thing it is ("A function that…"). The signature already shows it's a function.

**Spring (what happens after `return`):**
1. The `DispatcherServlet` receives the request and finds this function through its mapping.
2. The function returns a `List<InventoryItem>`.
3. Because of `@ResponseBody`, Spring picks a message converter that can write a list for the
   client's `Accept` header (MockMvc sends none, which means "anything"). Jackson's JSON
   converter matches, so the response gets `Content-Type: application/json`.
4. Jackson writes the list as a JSON array, one object per item, with the Kotlin property
   names as keys ([see InventoryItem](InventoryItem.kt.md)). An empty list becomes `[]`.

The status is `200 OK` because nothing threw and nothing set another status. If the database
fails, the exception passes through here untouched, and Spring Boot's error handling answers `500`
(see [why the service has no try/catch](InventoryService.kt.md#listinventory)).

**Kotlin:** an [expression body](../../test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md#the-container-bean)
again. The return type is written out, even though Kotlin could infer it from `listInventory()`.
On a public function that's the better choice: the signature shows what the endpoint returns
without anyone having to look at the service.

**Contract:** returning `List<InventoryItem>` is what makes the body "an array of `InventoryItem`".
The empty-array rule comes from the repository returning an empty list, and the SKU order from its
`ORDER BY sku_id`, not from anything here. The controller never sorts or filters.
`InventoryControllerTest` checks both cases with `JsonCompareMode.STRICT`.

### The second `// Contract:` comment

```kotlin
// Contract: paths./inventory/{skuId}.get - 200 application/json with InventoryItem, 404 with text/plain when SkuNotFoundException is thrown.
```

**Contract:** `paths./inventory/{skuId}.get` (`operationId: getInventory`) promises a `200` with an
`InventoryItem` as JSON, and a `404` whose body is the `Error` schema (a plain string) as
`text/plain` when "the SKU does not exist". The comment names both, and names the exception that
triggers the `404`, because nothing in this file produces it. A reader following the `404` needs
to know to look for `SkuNotFoundException`, which leads to the handler.

### `GET /inventory/{skuId}`

```kotlin
/** Returns an SKU and its quantity for GET /inventory/{skuId}. */
@GetMapping("/{skuId}")
fun getInventory(@PathVariable skuId: String): InventoryItem = inventoryService.getInventory(skuId)
```

**Spring (path templates):** `"/{skuId}"` is appended to the class's `/inventory`, giving
`/inventory/{skuId}`. The braces mark a **path variable**: that segment matches any text up to the
next `/`. So `/inventory/widget` matches with `skuId = "widget"`. `/inventory/widget/purchase` doesn't
match this mapping (it has one segment too many); that path will get its own mapping later.
`/inventory` alone still goes to `listInventory`, because it has no segment for `{skuId}`.

**Spring (`@PathVariable`):** tells Spring to fill this parameter from the path variable. With no
name given, it uses the **parameter's name**, so the Kotlin name `skuId` must match `{skuId}`
exactly. Spring can read Kotlin parameter names at runtime (the Spring Boot Gradle plugin turns on the
compiler's `javaParameters` option, and Spring can also read Kotlin's own metadata). If the names differed, you'd
write `@PathVariable("skuId") id: String`. Spring also URL-decodes the segment first, so a request
for `/inventory/caf%C3%A9` arrives as `café`.

**When a name mismatch fails** (walkthrough, 2026-09-28): `@GetMapping("/{skuId}")` with
`@PathVariable sku: String` compiles, because `"/{skuId}"` is just a string to the compiler, and the
app starts, because Spring doesn't compare placeholders with parameters when it registers the mapping.
It fails on the first request: Spring throws `MissingPathVariableException` and answers `500`, since
it's a server bug, not a client mistake. Only a test that sends a real request through MockMvc
catches it; calling `controller.getInventory("widget")` directly would skip path matching and pass.

**Kotlin (annotating a parameter):** an annotation can sit directly in front of a parameter,
inside the parentheses, the same as in Java.

**Kotlin + Spring (non-null `String`):** the parameter is `String`, not `String?`. A path variable is
always present when the mapping matches, so it can't be null, and the type says so. (A `String?`
parameter would tell Spring the value is optional.)

**Spring (the exception path):** when the service throws `SkuNotFoundException`, the exception passes
straight out of this function. Nothing is caught here. Spring's `DispatcherServlet` catches it,
asks its exception resolvers whether anyone handles that type, and finds
[`InventoryExceptionHandler.handleSkuNotFound`](error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt.md). Its
`ResponseEntity` becomes the response. Before the handler existed, nothing matched, so the exception
went up to the servlet container as a `500`. MockMvc has no container, so the tests saw it as a
`ServletException`.

**Why the function stays a one-liner:** Robert chose `@RestControllerAdvice` over building a
`ResponseEntity` here (2026-09-27). The controller keeps the happy path (return an `InventoryItem`,
Spring writes `200` JSON), and error mapping lives in one place for every endpoint. The rejected
version would have been an `if`/`?:` in this function that built a `404` `ResponseEntity`, with the
return type changed to `ResponseEntity<*>`. It can't be `ResponseEntity<InventoryItem>`, because
the error body is a `String`, not an `InventoryItem`, so the type would stop saying what the
endpoint returns.

**Naming:** `getInventory` matches the contract's `operationId: getInventory` and the service
function, the same one-name rule as `listInventory`. Kotlin allows it even though the class also has
a `listInventory`: the names differ. Overloading (two functions with the *same* name and different
parameters) would also be allowed, as in Java.

**Contract:** returning `InventoryItem` gives the `200` body `{"skuId": ..., "quantity": ...}`. A
sold-out SKU is still a row, so it comes back as `200` with `"quantity": 0`, never `404`
(`InventoryControllerTest` checks this).

### The third `// Contract:` comment

```kotlin
// Contract: paths./inventory/{skuId}.post - 200 application/json with InventoryItem, 400 text/plain for a quantity below 1, an unreadable body, the wrong Content-Type, or an add that would overflow.
```

**Contract:** `paths./inventory/{skuId}.post` (`operationId: createInventory`) lists two
responses: `200` with an `InventoryItem` as JSON ("the updated inventory state for the SKU"), and
`400` "Invalid request" as `text/plain`. The contract doesn't say *which* requests are invalid; the
four cases here are the README's "Contract gaps (POST)" decisions. Like the `404` comment above,
it names cases this file never handles itself, so a reader knows to look in the exception handler.
Robert's first version listed only the overflow case.

### `POST /inventory/{skuId}`

```kotlin
/** Adds quantity to the SKU's stock, creating the SKU if it's new, and returns the new total for POST /inventory/{skuId}.*/
@PostMapping("/{skuId}")
fun receiveInventory(@PathVariable skuId: String, @Valid @RequestBody requestQuantity: InventoryQuantity): InventoryItem = inventoryService.receiveInventory(skuId, requestQuantity.quantity)
```

**Spring (`@PostMapping`):** the `POST` version of [`@GetMapping`](#get-inventory), with the same
path template as `getInventory`. `GET` and `POST` to `/inventory/{skuId}` are two different
mappings, and Spring picks one by the HTTP method. `@PathVariable` works exactly as in
[`getInventory`](#get-inventoryskuid).

**Spring (`@RequestBody`):** fills this parameter from the request **body**. Spring picks a message
converter by the request's `Content-Type`: for `application/json` that's Jackson, which builds an
`InventoryQuantity` through its primary constructor (see
[InventoryQuantity](InventoryQuantity.kt.md#the-class)). It's the reverse of what
[`@ResponseBody`](#a-rest-controller-mapped-to-inventory) does with the return value.
`@RequestBody` is `required = true` by default, so a missing or `null` body is an error, matching
the contract's `requestBody: required: true`.

Unlike `@PathVariable`, the parameter **name** doesn't matter here: there's only one body, so
`requestQuantity` could be called anything. The JSON field names are matched against
`InventoryQuantity`'s properties, not against this parameter.

**Spring (`@Valid`):** tells Spring to run Bean Validation on the object after Jackson builds it.
That's what makes `@Min(1)` on `quantity` do anything. Without `@Valid`, `{"quantity": 0}` would
reach the service. (The service's own [`require`](InventoryService.kt.md#receiveinventory-a-precondition-and-a-block-body)
would then stop it, but as a `500`, not the contract's `400`.) The order of `@Valid` and
`@RequestBody` doesn't matter.

**Spring (what happens before this function runs):** the function body only runs if all of this
succeeds. Each step that fails throws an exception, and the function is never called:

| Step | Fails when | Exception | Handler's response |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Find a converter for the `Content-Type` | not JSON, e.g. `text/plain` | `HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException` | `400 Content-Type must be application/json` |
| 2. Jackson reads the body into `InventoryQuantity` | empty, malformed, wrong type, too big, `null` | `HttpMessageNotReadableException` | `400 Invalid request body` |
| 3. `@Valid` runs Bean Validation | `quantity < 1` | `MethodArgumentNotValidException` | `400 quantity must be at least 1` |
| 4. The function calls the service | the total would overflow | `AddStockOverflowException` | `400 Quantity would exceed the maximum stock` |

Steps 1 to 3 are Spring's own exceptions. Without handlers, Spring's built-in resolver answers them
(`415` for step 1, a `400` for steps 2 and 3, with Spring Boot's JSON error body in the running app
and an empty body under MockMvc, never the contract's `text/plain` string); the
[exception handler](error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt.md) overrides that to match the contract.

**Why the service gets `requestQuantity.quantity`, not the object:** the request body is an HTTP
shape. The service takes plain `String` + `Int` and never depends on a web class (see the
[service notes](InventoryService.kt.md#receiveinventory-a-precondition-and-a-block-body)). Robert's
first version passed a bare `quantity`, which doesn't exist in this scope: the `Int` is inside
the object, so it has to be read with `.quantity`.

**Why `200` and not `201 Created`:** a `POST` that creates something is often a `201`. The contract
lists only `200`, for both "created" and "added to", and the tests check it. Returning
`InventoryItem` (not a `ResponseEntity`) gives Spring's default `200`.

**Where is the 200 enforced?** (walkthrough, 2026-09-29) Nowhere in production code: it's a
default. Getting `201` would take `@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)` on the function, or a
`ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED)` return. What pins the `200` is the test:
`status { isOk() }` in `InventoryControllerTest`'s `POST inventory creates a new SKU`. Defaults
don't show up in code, so a test has to pin them.

**Naming:** `receiveInventory` matches the service function, the "one name through the layers" rule.
It does *not* match the contract's `operationId: createInventory`: this endpoint creates **or**
adds, and "receive" (from the brief's "receiving new stock") covers both. Robert's first name,
`postInventory`, described the HTTP verb rather than the action, and shared its name with the test
helper, which made the tests confusing to read.

**Kotlin:** an expression body again, with a missing `:` before the return type in Robert's first
version (`fun f(...) InventoryItem = ...` doesn't compile).

**Contract:** the body is an `InventoryItem`: `RETURNING` in the repository gives the row as it is
after the change, so the response is the new total. `InventoryControllerTest` checks both a new
SKU (`10`) and an existing one (`5 + 3 = 8`) with `JsonCompareMode.STRICT`.

# InventoryExceptionHandler.kt

> Source: [src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt](../../../../../../src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-28

## Role

Written by Robert. It turns exceptions into HTTP error responses. It sits *beside* the request flow,
not in it. It handles five exceptions of two kinds: ours, thrown by the service, and Spring's own,
thrown while Spring reads the request, before the controller function runs. Without this class,
ours would become `500`s and Spring's would get Spring's default `400` or `415`, never the
contract's `text/plain` text.

| Exception | From | Response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`SkuNotFoundException`](SkuNotFoundException.kt.md) | our service | `404` `SKU not found: <skuId>` |
| [`AddStockOverflowException`](AddStockOverflowException.kt.md) | our service | `400` `Quantity would exceed the maximum stock` |
| `MethodArgumentNotValidException` | Spring (Bean Validation) | `400` with the `@Min` message |
| `HttpMessageNotReadableException` | Spring (Jackson) | `400` `Invalid request body` |
| `HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException` | Spring (content negotiation) | `400` `Content-Type must be application/json` |

Every body is `text/plain`. The purchase endpoint will add its own handlers here, so every error body
the contract requires is built in one file.

## Walkthrough

### Imports

```kotlin
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus
import org.springframework.http.MediaType
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity
import org.springframework.http.converter.HttpMessageNotReadableException
import org.springframework.web.HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException
import org.springframework.web.bind.MethodArgumentNotValidException
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.ExceptionHandler
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestControllerAdvice
```

**Kotlin:** `SkuNotFoundException` and `AddStockOverflowException` are in the same package
(`inventory.error`), so they need no import. The three Spring exceptions do. Robert's first
`MethodArgumentNotValidException` handler didn't compile for exactly this reason: his own exceptions
had never needed an import, so the rule hadn't come up.
`org.springframework.http` holds the HTTP building blocks (status codes, media types, responses);
`web.bind.annotation` holds the Spring MVC annotations, the same package as `@GetMapping`. Note
`web.bind` (the exception) vs `web.bind.annotation` (the annotations): two different packages.

### The class, and why it's an advice

```kotlin
// Why: RestController advice so spring will catch and return specific responses we have built out for every controller rather than us building out multiple response entities for each controller. We rejected ResponseStatusException because its body is JSON, not text/plain.

/** Where the various custom built exceptions and spring exceptions are transformed to HTTP responses. */
@RestControllerAdvice
class InventoryExceptionHandler{
```

**Spring (`@RestControllerAdvice`):** it's `@ControllerAdvice` plus `@ResponseBody`, the same pairing
as [`@RestController`](../InventoryController.kt.md#a-rest-controller-mapped-to-inventory).
- `@ControllerAdvice` is a stereotype (it's annotated with `@Component`), so component scanning makes
  this class a bean at startup. Spring MVC then remembers it as a source of `@ExceptionHandler`
  methods that apply to **every** controller.
- `@ResponseBody` means a handler's return value is written as the response body. Here the return
  type is `ResponseEntity`, which is always written as the response anyway, so this half isn't
  strictly needed. It would matter for a handler that returned a plain `String`.

Think of it as one `try`/`catch` that Spring wraps around every controller method, written once
instead of in each controller.

**Why:** the `// Why:` records Robert's decision (2026-09-27). The two rejected options:
- **A `ResponseEntity` built in the controller.** The controller would need an `if`/`?:` and a
  `ResponseEntity<*>` return type, and every endpoint that can miss a SKU (purchase too) would repeat
  it. With the advice, controllers keep the happy path only.
- **`ResponseStatusException`.** The service would throw an exception that carries an HTTP status,
  so HTTP knowledge would leak into the service layer. That's the stronger reason. The body is
  also wrong by default: Spring Boot renders it through its error page, which means JSON for API
  clients, an HTML page for browsers, and an empty body under MockMvc (no error page there). None
  of these is the contract's `text/plain` string. (An advice *could* catch `ResponseStatusException`
  and write text itself, but then the custom exception is simpler.) The `// Why:` comment's "its body is
  JSON" is the common case, not the whole story.

**Placement:** the `// Why:` sits above the KDoc, with a blank line between, so the KDoc stays
directly on the class. Robert's first version put the comment between the KDoc and
`@RestControllerAdvice`. That cuts the KDoc off from the class: it no longer shows on hover, and
`check_kdoc.py` flagged the class as undocumented.

**Kotlin:** no constructor parameters, because the handler needs nothing injected. A class with no
primary constructor parameters is declared with just its name, as here. Spring calls its no-argument
constructor. `InventoryExceptionHandler{` with no space is legal.

### The `// Contract:` comment

```kotlin
// Contract: paths./inventory/{skuId}.get - 404 with text/plain when SkuNotFoundException is thrown.
```

**Contract:** `paths./inventory/{skuId}.get`, response `'404'`: content `text/plain`, schema
`#/components/schemas/Error` (`type: string`). This comment is the other end of the one in the
[controller](../InventoryController.kt.md#the-second--contract-comment): the controller says the `404`
comes from `SkuNotFoundException`, and this file is where it's produced.

### `handleSkuNotFound`

```kotlin
/** Returns a 404 text/plain response whose body is the exception's message. */
@ExceptionHandler(SkuNotFoundException::class)
fun handleSkuNotFound(ex: SkuNotFoundException ): ResponseEntity<String> =

    ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
        .contentType(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
        .body(ex.message ?: "SKU not found.")
```

**Spring (`@ExceptionHandler`):** registers this function for `SkuNotFoundException` (and any
subclass of it). When a controller method throws, Spring's `DispatcherServlet` asks its exception
resolvers for a match, in this order:
1. an `@ExceptionHandler` inside the controller class itself,
2. then `@ExceptionHandler`s in `@ControllerAdvice` beans, like this one,
3. then `@ResponseStatus` on the exception class and `ResponseStatusException`,
4. then Spring's built-in mappings (e.g. a malformed request → `400`),
5. and if nothing matches, a `500` with Spring Boot's default JSON error body.

Spring catches *every* exception, custom or not: the advice isn't where Spring looks when it
"doesn't recognize" an exception (the 2026-09-28 walkthrough's first framing). It just gets a
custom exception handled at step 2 instead of falling through to the `500` at step 5.

Within one class, if several handlers match, the one for the *closest* exception type wins, so a
later `@ExceptionHandler(RuntimeException::class)` in this class wouldn't steal this one's
exceptions. Across several advice classes, their order (`@Order`) decides first: the first advice
with *any* matching handler wins. Spring passes the thrown exception in as the
parameter, and the function's return value becomes the response.

`SkuNotFoundException::class` is a [class reference](../../../test/InventoryApplicationTests.kt.md#starting-the-real-application-in-a-test),
Kotlin's `SkuNotFoundException.class`.

**Spring (`ResponseEntity` builder):** `ResponseEntity` is a whole HTTP response: status, headers and
body. It's built with a chain where each call returns a builder, and the last call produces the
response:

| Call | Sets | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)` | status `404` | a `BodyBuilder` |
| `.contentType(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)` | the `Content-Type` header | the same `BodyBuilder` |
| `.body(...)` | the body | `ResponseEntity<String>` |

The body's type becomes the `T` in `ResponseEntity<T>`, which is why the return type is
`ResponseEntity<String>`. Spring then writes the `String` as-is with its `StringHttpMessageConverter`
(no JSON quotes around it).

Two things this chain avoids:
- **`ResponseEntity.notFound()`** looks like a shortcut, but it returns a `HeadersBuilder`, which has
  no `.body(...)`. Only `.build()`, giving an empty `404`.
- **Leaving out `.contentType(...)`.** Spring would then choose the type from the request's
  `Accept` header, and could send `application/json` for a client that asks for JSON. Setting it
  here makes the `text/plain` promise hold for every client.

Robert's first version used `HttpStatus.CONFLICT` (409), copied from a parallel example. Both
`404` tests caught it: `Status expected:<404> but was:<409>`.

**Kotlin (`message` is nullable):** `ex.message` comes from Java's `Throwable.getMessage()`, which
may return null, so Kotlin types it `String?`. `body(...)` here needs a `String`, so the null case
must be handled. The [Elvis operator](../InventoryService.kt.md#getinventory-turning-no-row-into-an-error)
gives a fallback. The three options that were weighed:

| Option | If `message` were null | Chosen? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ex.message ?: "SKU not found."` | a readable fallback body | **yes** |
| `ex.message!!` | throws a `NullPointerException` inside the error handler | no |
| keep `skuId` as a `val` on the exception and build the text here | can't be null | no |

In practice the fallback never runs: `SkuNotFoundException`'s constructor always passes
`"SKU not found: $skuId"`, so `message` is never null. The `?:` is there because the compiler can't
see that. Robert chose a readable fallback over an empty string (2026-09-27), because a client
getting an empty `404` body would have nothing to go on.

**Worth knowing: handled exceptions aren't logged.** Once this handler returns, Spring treats the
exception as dealt with and logs nothing at the default log level. The fallback text only ever
reaches the API client. If missing SKUs should show up in the logs, that's a logger call in this
function.

**Worth knowing: no charset in the header.** Checked against the running app on 2026-09-27:
`curl -i http://localhost:8080/inventory/missing` returns `Content-Type: text/plain`, with no
`charset` parameter, while the body bytes are UTF-8 (a SKU `café` comes back as UTF-8 bytes). For
ASCII SKUs this makes no difference. A client that assumes a different charset could misread
non-ASCII ones. `MediaType("text", "plain", Charsets.UTF_8)` would state it; this is tracked in TODO.

**Kotlin:** an [expression body](../../../test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md#the-container-bean)
split across lines. The blank line after `=` is legal, and each line starting with `.` continues the
chain. The space in `SkuNotFoundException )` changes nothing.

**Naming:** `handle` + what went wrong is the usual Spring convention, so each function name says
which case it covers. Robert first reused the class name, `inventoryExceptionHandler`, and renamed
it in review.

**Contract:** status `404`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, and a body that is a bare string: the `Error`
schema is `type: string`, not an object. `InventoryControllerTest` checks all three, with
`contentTypeCompatibleWith(TEXT_PLAIN)` so a later `;charset=UTF-8` would still pass.

### `handleStockOverflow`: our exception, our message
