```kotlin
/** Returns a 400 text/plain response whose body is the exception's message.*/
@ExceptionHandler(AddStockOverflowException::class)
fun handleStockOverflow(ex: AddStockOverflowException): ResponseEntity<String> =

    ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST)
        .contentType(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
        .body(ex.message ?: "Overflow Guard Triggered")
```

**Spring:** the same shape as `handleSkuNotFound`, with `HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST` (`400`) instead of
`NOT_FOUND`. Robert's first version kept `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` from an earlier draft; the overflow
test caught it (`Status expected:<400> but was:<500>`). Each `HttpStatus` constant is just a name
for a number, and the client gets whatever is passed to `status(...)`.

**Why `ex.message` is safe here:** we wrote this exception's message for the client
(`"Quantity would exceed the maximum stock"`, in
[AddStockOverflowException](AddStockOverflowException.kt.md)). As with `SkuNotFoundException`, the
`?:` fallback never runs; it's only there because `Throwable.message` is typed `String?`.

**Contract:** `paths./inventory/{skuId}.post`, response `'400'`, `text/plain`. The overflow case
itself is a README "Contract gaps (POST)" decision.

### `handleValidationFailure`: the message from `@Min`

```kotlin
// Contract: paths./inventory/{skuId}.post - a request body that fails validation is a 400 text/plain.

/** Returns a 400 text/plain response from the failing field's validation message.*/
@ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException::class)
fun handleValidationFailure(ex: MethodArgumentNotValidException): ResponseEntity<String> =

    ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST)
        .contentType(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
        .body(ex.bindingResult.fieldError?.defaultMessage ?: "Invalid request")
```

**Spring (handling Spring's own exceptions):** `MethodArgumentNotValidException` is what
`@Valid @RequestBody` throws when Bean Validation fails. An advice doesn't care whose exception it
handles. Because `@ExceptionHandler` methods in advice are tried (step 2 in the list above) before
Spring's built-in mappings (step 4), this handler replaces Spring's default answer: a `400` without
our text (Spring Boot's JSON error body in the running app, an empty body under MockMvc).

**Why not `ex.message`:** for Spring's exceptions the message is written for developers, not
clients. Robert's first version returned it, and the test showed what the client would have got:

```text
Validation failed for argument [1] in public com.robertwoolbright.inventory.inventory.InventoryItem
com.robertwoolbright.inventory.inventory.InventoryController.receiveInventory(java.lang.String,...
```

That leaks the package, class and method names to anyone calling the API. The `?:` fallback didn't
help either: `?:` only runs when the left side is `null`, and Spring's messages never are.

**Kotlin (a chain of safe calls):** the message the client should see is the one in
`@Min(message = ...)`. Spring stores it on the exception:

| Expression | Type | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ex.bindingResult` | `BindingResult` | every validation error for the body |
| `.fieldError` | `FieldError?` | the first error on a field; `null` if none |
| `?.defaultMessage` | `String?` | that error's message, here `"quantity must be at least 1"` |
| `?: "Invalid request"` | `String` | the fallback if anything above was `null` |

`?.` is the **safe-call operator**: `a?.b` is `a.b` if `a` isn't `null`, and `null` if it is, instead
of a `NullPointerException`. One `?:` at the end covers a `null` from any step in the chain. Java
equivalent:

```java
FieldError error = ex.getBindingResult().getFieldError();
String message = (error != null && error.getDefaultMessage() != null)
        ? error.getDefaultMessage() : "Invalid request";
```

Both `fieldError` and `defaultMessage` are Java getters marked `@Nullable` in Spring, so Kotlin
types them `T?` and the compiler insists on `?.` (see [platform types](../../../build.gradle.kts.md#compiler-options)).

**Why read it from the exception, not hardcode it:** Robert's second version returned the fixed text
`"quantity must be at least 1"`. The tests passed, but the text then lived in two places, and the
handler would say "quantity must be at least 1" for *any* validation failure, including rules added
later. Reading `defaultMessage` keeps the annotation as the single source of the text.

**Only the first error:** `fieldError` returns one error. The request body has one field today, so
there's only ever one. With several fields, the client would see the first failure only.

**Naming:** first `handleMalformedBody` (wrong: a malformed body is the next handler's job), then
`handleMinQuantity`, renamed in review to `handleValidationFailure`, because the advice is global
and will catch every Bean Validation failure on any `@Valid` body, not just `@Min`. The fallback and
KDoc were made general at the same time. Spring never calls the method by name, so the rename
couldn't change behavior.

### `handleInvalidRequestBody`: a handler with no parameters

```kotlin
// Contract: paths./inventory/{skuId}.post - when the request body is invalid we return a 400 text/plain.

/** Returns a 400 text/plain response with the fixed text Invalid request body.*/
@ExceptionHandler(HttpMessageNotReadableException::class)
fun handleInvalidRequestBody(): ResponseEntity<String> =

    ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST)
        .contentType(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
        .body("Invalid request body")
```

**Spring:** `HttpMessageNotReadableException` covers every way reading the body can fail: empty,
malformed JSON, `null`, an array, a missing or `null` `quantity`, a string, a decimal, or a number too
big for `Int` (the nine cases in
[InventoryControllerTest](../../../test/inventory/InventoryControllerTest.kt.md#every-unreadable-body-is-a-400)).
They all get the same fixed text, the README "Contract gaps (POST)" decision.

**Why a fixed string:** the exception's message is Jackson's, for example
`JSON parse error: Cannot coerce String value ("5") to 'int' value (but might if coercion using 'CoercionConfig' was enabled)`.
It names internal settings and differs for every case. There's nothing useful in it for the client
that "Invalid request body" doesn't say.

**Spring (no parameters):** once the body doesn't need the exception, the parameter can go. The
exception type in `@ExceptionHandler(...)` is what routes the exception here; the parameter is only
there when you want to *read* it. Spring looks at the parameter list, finds nothing to fill in, and
calls the function with no arguments. With the parameter gone, the signature itself shows which
handlers use the exception and which don't. Robert's first try removed only the name, leaving
`(HttpMessageNotReadableException)`. Kotlin reads that as a parameter *named*
`HttpMessageNotReadableException` with no type: "An explicit type is required on a value parameter".
A parameter is always `name: Type`, in Java too.

### `handleContentTypeMismatch`: 400 instead of Spring's 415

```kotlin
// Contract: paths./inventory/{skuId}.post - when the content type is not application/json we return a 400 text/plain.

/** Returns a 400 text/plain response with the fixed text Content-Type must be application/json.*/
@ExceptionHandler(HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException::class)
fun handleContentTypeMismatch():ResponseEntity<String> =

    ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST)
        .contentType(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
        .body("Content-Type must be application/json")
```

**Spring:** `@RequestBody` throws `HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException` when no message converter can
read the request's `Content-Type` into `InventoryQuantity` (only Jackson can, and only for JSON).
Spring's default answer is `415 Unsupported Media Type`: correct HTTP, but the contract lists only
`200` and `400`. This handler overrides it.

Robert's first version returned `HttpStatus.UNSUPPORTED_MEDIA_TYPE` here, so the handler *was*
running but sent `415` on purpose. The status comes from the code, not from the exception.

**Why:** a `415` is arguably the better HTTP answer, but a client written against the contract
only expects `200` or `400`. Sticking to the contract was the README decision (2026-09-28).

**Spring (global reach):** like every handler here, this one applies to every controller. Any future
endpoint with a `@RequestBody` gets the same `400` for a non-JSON request, which is what we want.

**Kotlin:** `():ResponseEntity<String>` with no spaces is legal. Robert's first version also copied
the body from the handler above (`"Invalid request body"`); the test caught the wrong text.

## Check your understanding

- Remove `@RestControllerAdvice` and run `GET /inventory/missing`. What status comes back, and why
  does the handler function no longer run?
- A second handler, `@ExceptionHandler(RuntimeException::class)`, is added to this class. Which
  handler answers a missing SKU, and which answers a database failure?
- What would the client receive with `ResponseEntity.notFound().build()` instead of the chain?
- Why does `ex.message` need `?:` even though the message can never be null here?
- `handleInvalidRequestBody` returned `ex.message ?: "Invalid request body"`. What would the client see for `{"quantity": "5"}`, and why does the fallback never appear?
- Delete `handleContentTypeMismatch`. What does a `text/plain` POST get now, and which part of Spring produces it?
- What does `ex.bindingResult.fieldError?.defaultMessage` evaluate to for `{"quantity": 0}`? When would the `?:` fallback be used?
- Why is `ex.message` fine to send for `AddStockOverflowException` but not for `HttpMessageNotReadableException`?

# Nuuly Inventory API

A small inventory-management REST API built for the Nuuly services assessment. It
receives stock by SKU, processes purchases without overselling, and reports current
inventory levels.

The API contract is [src/main/resources/openapi/inventory.yaml](src/main/resources/openapi/inventory.yaml)
(OpenAPI 3.0.3), and the implementation must conform to it exactly. The original brief
is in [docs/Nuuly_Assessment_Instructions.txt](docs/Nuuly_Assessment_Instructions.txt).

## Endpoints

| Method | Path | Behavior | Responses | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/inventory` | List every SKU and its quantity (`[]` when empty) | `200` JSON array | Implemented; tests green; reviewed and walked through |
| `GET` | `/inventory/{skuId}` | Current quantity for one SKU (`404` body: `SKU not found: <skuId>`) | `200` JSON, `404` text | Implemented; tests green; reviewed and walked through |
| `POST` | `/inventory/{skuId}` | Add stock; creates the SKU if it is new (one atomic upsert) | `200` JSON, `400` text | Implemented; tests green; reviewed; walkthrough pending |
| `POST` | `/inventory/{skuId}/purchase` | Deduct stock, only if enough is on hand | `200` JSON, `400` / `404` text | Not started |

Request bodies are `{"quantity": <integer ≥ 1>}`. Success bodies are
`{"skuId": "...", "quantity": <integer ≥ 0>}`. Error bodies are plain-text strings
(`text/plain`), not JSON.

## Open decisions

These are settled one at a time before the code that depends on them is written.
Each decision and its reasoning is recorded here once it is made.

| Decision | Options under consideration | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data store | **PostgreSQL**, run with Docker Compose. Considered in-memory and H2; see below. | Decided 2026-09-23 |
| Concurrency on purchase | **Single atomic SQL statements** + `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` backstop. See below. | Decided 2026-09-23 |
| Data-access library | **`JdbcClient`**: explicit SQL, maps to immutable data classes. Considered Spring Data JDBC, Spring Data JPA, Exposed. | Decided 2026-09-23 |
| Controllers | **Hand-written**, plus a contract-validation test (responses checked against `inventory.yaml`). Considered generating them with `openapi-generator`, but that hides the Spring MVC wiring and is overkill for 4 endpoints. | Decided 2026-09-23 |
| Schema migrations | **Flyway**: versioned plain-SQL files, run automatically at startup and in tests. Considered Liquibase (XML/YAML changesets, more ceremony) and `schema.sql` (no versioning). | Decided 2026-09-23 |
| List order and contents | **Ordered by `sku_id`** (the contract specifies no order; a fixed one keeps responses and tests stable). **Zero-stock SKUs are listed**: a sold-out SKU still exists, and `GET /inventory/{skuId}` returns it with quantity `0`. | Decided 2026-09-24 |
| Column types | `sku_id TEXT` (exact, case-sensitive match for now), `quantity INTEGER` (Kotlin `Int`). Considered `BIGINT`/`Long`; overflow will be handled when adding stock instead. | Decided 2026-09-24 |
| Error handling | A domain exception per error (`SkuNotFoundException`, `AddStockOverflowException`), thrown by the service and mapped to a `text/plain` response by one `@RestControllerAdvice`. The same advice maps Spring's request-reading exceptions for `POST` (`MethodArgumentNotValidException`, `HttpMessageNotReadableException`, `HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException`) to `400`s, and never sends Spring's own exception messages to the client (2026-09-28). Exceptions and the handler live in the `inventory.error` subpackage. 404 body: `SKU not found: <skuId>`, no trailing period. Considered a `ResponseEntity` built in each controller (repeats per endpoint), `ResponseStatusException` (JSON body, the contract needs `text/plain`), and a flat or top-level `error` package. | Decided 2026-09-27 |
| Demo seed data | Tests insert their own rows. Whether a running app should start with sample data (e.g. a dev-only Flyway location) is decided once `POST /inventory/{skuId}` exists. | Open |
| Contract gaps (POST) | Settled for `POST /inventory/{skuId}` by Robert on 2026-09-28. **SKU ids: exact, case-sensitive match** (`W` and `w` are two SKUs; the contract sets no format, and normalizing would silently change the id a client sent). **Strict JSON:** malformed, empty or `null` bodies, a missing or `null` `quantity`, a string (`"5"`), a decimal (`1.5`) or a number too big for `Int` are all `400` `Invalid request body` (Jackson's lenient defaults would coerce `"5"` and truncate `1.5`). `quantity < 1`: `400` `quantity must be at least 1`, checked with Bean Validation in the controller layer (considered a manual check in the service). The service also has `require(quantity >= 1)` for callers that bypass HTTP; hitting it is our bug, so it's a `500`, not a `400` (added in review, 2026-09-28). **Wrong `Content-Type`:** `400` `Content-Type must be application/json` instead of Spring's `415`, which the contract doesn't list. **Overflow:** a total past `Int.MAX_VALUE` is `400` `Quantity would exceed the maximum stock`, refused atomically inside the upsert's SQL (considered leaving Postgres's `integer out of range` as a `500`). All `400` bodies are `text/plain`. | Decided 2026-09-28 |

### Decision record: PostgreSQL and atomic SQL

The key requirement is that **a purchase must never oversell, even when requests arrive at
the same moment.** In PostgreSQL, each write is a single atomic statement, so the database
guarantees this without any locking code in the application:

```sql
-- Receive stock: create the SKU or add to it
INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity) VALUES (?, ?)
ON CONFLICT (sku_id) DO UPDATE SET quantity = inventory.quantity + EXCLUDED.quantity
RETURNING sku_id, quantity;

-- Purchase: succeeds only if enough stock exists (0 rows updated -> 404 or 400)
UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - ?
WHERE sku_id = ? AND quantity >= ?
RETURNING sku_id, quantity;
```

There is no read-then-write race, and correctness still holds with several instances of the
service running. A `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` constraint is a second line of defense.

Alternatives we rejected:

- **In-memory map:** needs no setup, but data is lost on restart and it only works with a
  single instance.
- **H2:** its SQL dialect differs from production databases.
- **Redis / document stores:** add nothing for a single integer per key.

Kotlin doesn't favor any particular database; it uses the same JDBC drivers as Java. It does
favor data-access libraries that work with immutable `data class`es (`JdbcClient`, Spring Data
JDBC, Exposed) over JPA, which needs compiler plugins to work around Kotlin's final-by-default classes.

The oversell guarantee is tested with several different mechanisms: race tests, a negative
control, multi-instance tests, load tests and property-based tests. The full plan is in
[.claude/TODO.md](.claude/TODO.md#oversell-protection-test-plan).

| List order and contents | **Ordered by `sku_id`** (the contract specifies no order; a fixed one keeps responses and tests stable). **Zero-stock SKUs are listed**: a sold-out SKU still exists, and `GET /inventory/{skuId}` returns it with quantity `0`. | Decided 2026-09-24 |
| Column types | `sku_id TEXT` (exact, case-sensitive match for now), `quantity INTEGER` (Kotlin `Int`). Considered `BIGINT`/`Long`; overflow will be handled when adding stock instead. | Decided 2026-09-24 |
| Error handling | A domain exception per error (`SkuNotFoundException`, `AddStockOverflowException`), thrown by the service and mapped to a `text/plain` response by one `@RestControllerAdvice`. The same advice maps Spring's request-reading exceptions for `POST` (`MethodArgumentNotValidException`, `HttpMessageNotReadableException`, `HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException`) to `400`s, and never sends Spring's own exception messages to the client (2026-09-28). Exceptions and the handler live in the `inventory.error` subpackage. 404 body: `SKU not found: <skuId>`, no trailing period. Considered a `ResponseEntity` built in each controller (repeats per endpoint), `ResponseStatusException` (JSON body, the contract needs `text/plain`), and a flat or top-level `error` package. | Decided 2026-09-27 |
| Demo seed data | Tests insert their own rows. Whether a running app should start with sample data (e.g. a dev-only Flyway location) is decided once `POST /inventory/{skuId}` exists. | Open |
| Contract gaps (POST) | Settled for `POST /inventory/{skuId}` by Robert on 2026-09-28. **SKU ids: exact, case-sensitive match** (`W` and `w` are two SKUs; the contract sets no format, and normalizing would silently change the id a client sent). **Strict JSON:** malformed, empty or `null` bodies, a missing or `null` `quantity`, a string (`"5"`), a decimal (`1.5`) or a number too big for `Int` are all `400` `Invalid request body` (Jackson's lenient defaults would coerce `"5"` and truncate `1.5`). `quantity < 1`: `400` `quantity must be at least 1`, checked with Bean Validation in the controller layer (considered a manual check in the service). The service also has `require(quantity >= 1)` for callers that bypass HTTP; hitting it is our bug, so it's a `500`, not a `400` (added in review, 2026-09-28). **Wrong `Content-Type`:** `400` `Content-Type must be application/json` instead of Spring's `415`, which the contract doesn't list. **Overflow:** a total past `Int.MAX_VALUE` is `400` `Quantity would exceed the maximum stock`, refused atomically inside the upsert's SQL (considered leaving Postgres's `integer out of range` as a `500`). All `400` bodies are `text/plain`. | Decided 2026-09-28 |

### Decision record: PostgreSQL and atomic SQL

The key requirement is that **a purchase must never oversell, even when requests arrive at
the same moment.** In PostgreSQL, each write is a single atomic statement, so the database
guarantees this without any locking code in the application:

```sql
-- Receive stock: create the SKU or add to it
INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity) VALUES (?, ?)
ON CONFLICT (sku_id) DO UPDATE SET quantity = inventory.quantity + EXCLUDED.quantity
RETURNING sku_id, quantity;

-- Purchase: succeeds only if enough stock exists (0 rows updated -> 404 or 400)
UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - ?
WHERE sku_id = ? AND quantity >= ?
RETURNING sku_id, quantity;
```

There is no read-then-write race, and correctness still holds with several instances of the
service running. A `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` constraint is a second line of defense.

Alternatives we rejected:

- **In-memory map:** needs no setup, but data is lost on restart and it only works with a
  single instance.
- **H2:** its SQL dialect differs from production databases.
- **Redis / document stores:** add nothing for a single integer per key.

Kotlin doesn't favor any particular database; it uses the same JDBC drivers as Java. It does
favor data-access libraries that work with immutable `data class`es (`JdbcClient`, Spring Data
JDBC, Exposed) over JPA, which needs compiler plugins to work around Kotlin's final-by-default classes.

The oversell guarantee is tested with several different mechanisms: race tests, a negative
control, multi-instance tests, load tests and property-based tests. The full plan is in
[.claude/TODO.md](.claude/TODO.md#oversell-protection-test-plan).

# PurchaseResult.kt

> Source: [src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/PurchaseResult.kt](../../../../../src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/PurchaseResult.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-29

## Role

Robert wrote this type. It is the answer the [repository's `removeStock`](InventoryRepository.kt.md#removestock-three-outcomes-from-one-statement)
gives the [service's `purchaseInventory`](InventoryService.kt.md#purchaseinventory-one-branch-per-outcome).
A purchase can end in three ways, and the API answers each one differently:

| Case | Meaning | Service does | Client gets |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Purchased(item)` | the SKU had enough stock, and it was deducted | returns `item` | `200` with the remaining stock |
| `SkuNotFound` | there is no row for that SKU | throws `SkuNotFoundException` | `404` |
| `InsufficientStock` | the row exists but holds less than requested | throws `InsufficientInventoryException` | `400` |

This file contains no logic. It only names the three outcomes, so the repository can report what the
SQL found without deciding what that means for HTTP.

## Walkthrough

### Why a new type at all

```kotlin
// Why: We used the sealed interface because we have 3 possible outcomes we need to account for. Not just a success or null so returning InventoryItem? doesn't help us between when we need to throw 404 or 400.
```

**Why:** `addStock` has two outcomes, a row or a refusal, so it returns
[`InventoryItem?`](InventoryRepository.kt.md#findbyskuid-a-nullable-return-type) and uses `null`
for the refusal. A purchase has two different failures. If `removeStock` returned `InventoryItem?`,
a `null` couldn't say which failure happened, and the service would have to go back to the database
to find out. That second query is a race: another request could create or change the SKU between
the two queries. The decision (Robert, 2026-09-29) was to have one SQL statement work out the
outcome, and one type that carries each outcome separately.

Alternatives that were considered:
- **Throw from the repository.** This would work, but then the repository decides what counts as
  an error, which is the service's job (see
  [why throw in the service](InventoryService.kt.md#getinventory-turning-no-row-into-an-error)).
- **An `enum` plus a nullable item.** `enum class Outcome { PURCHASED, NOT_FOUND, INSUFFICIENT }`
  can't carry the item, so it would need a separate `item: InventoryItem?` next to it. The compiler
  couldn't then guarantee that `PURCHASED` always comes with an item.

### A sealed interface

```kotlin
/** PurchaseResult is returned by the repository and translated by the service. */
sealed interface PurchaseResult {
```

**Kotlin (`interface`):** a Kotlin interface works like a Java interface: a type that other classes
implement. This one has no members at all. It exists only so the three cases share one type, which
lets `removeStock` declare a single return type, `PurchaseResult`.

**Kotlin (`sealed`):** `sealed` closes the list of implementations. Every class that implements
`PurchaseResult` must be declared in the same package and the same module (for this project, the
`inventory` package inside this Gradle build). No other code can add a fourth case. The compiler
therefore knows the complete list, and that is what makes the service's `when` work without an
`else` branch (see [exhaustive `when`](InventoryService.kt.md#purchaseinventory-one-branch-per-outcome)).
If someone later adds a fourth case here, every `when` over `PurchaseResult` that lacks an `else`
stops compiling until it handles the new case. A type change produces a list of every place that
needs updating.

**Java equivalent:** Java 17 has the same feature, where the class must list its permitted subtypes:

```java
public sealed interface PurchaseResult
        permits PurchaseResult.Purchased, PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound, PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock {
    record Purchased(InventoryItem item) implements PurchaseResult {}
    final class SkuNotFound implements PurchaseResult { /* a singleton, by hand */ }
    final class InsufficientStock implements PurchaseResult { /* a singleton, by hand */ }
}
```

Kotlin doesn't need a `permits` list. Its rule is simpler: anything declared in the same package
and module is allowed.

**Sealed interface or sealed class:** `sealed class PurchaseResult` would also work. An interface
fits better here because the cases share no state or code. A class can extend only one class but
can implement many interfaces, so using an interface keeps that option open.

### The success case: a `data class`

```kotlin
/** The SKU exists and had enough stock. Item holds the remaining stock. */
data class Purchased(val item: InventoryItem) : PurchaseResult
```

**Kotlin (nested classes):** `Purchased` is declared *inside* `PurchaseResult`, so its full name is
`PurchaseResult.Purchased`, and that is how the repository and the service refer to it. Nesting
keeps the three cases grouped under the type they belong to. A nested class in Kotlin is like a
`static` nested class in Java: it has no hidden link to an outer object. (Kotlin's `inner` keyword
would add that link. It isn't needed here, and an interface has no instance to link to anyway.)

**Kotlin (`data class`):** the same feature as [`InventoryItem`](InventoryItem.kt.md). The
generated `equals` is what lets the repository test compare a whole result in one line:
`assertEquals(PurchaseResult.Purchased(InventoryItem("widget", 3)), removeStock(...))`.

**Kotlin (`: PurchaseResult`):** this declares that `Purchased` implements the interface. Because
it's an interface, there are no parentheses after the name: there's no constructor to call. Compare
with [`: RuntimeException(...)`](error/SkuNotFoundException.kt.md#the-whole-class-in-one-line), which
extends a class and therefore calls its constructor.

**Why it carries an `InventoryItem`:** a successful purchase has data, the remaining stock, and
the service returns it as the `200` body. The two failures have no data, so they don't need a class
with properties.

### The failure cases: `data object`

```kotlin
/** There's no row for that SKU id. */
data object SkuNotFound : PurchaseResult

/** The row exists but has less than the requested quantity. */
data object InsufficientStock : PurchaseResult
```

**Kotlin (`object`):** `object` declares a class and creates its only instance in one step, which
makes it a **singleton**. There is exactly one `SkuNotFound` in the program, and code refers to it
by name without `()`: `PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound`, never `PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound()`. A case
that carries no data doesn't need a new object each time.

**Kotlin (`data object`):** adding `data` gives the object a readable `toString()`, `"SkuNotFound"`,
instead of the default `PurchaseResult$SkuNotFound@1b6d3586`. That shows up in test failure
messages: `expected:<InsufficientStock> but was:<SkuNotFound>`. It also generates `equals` and
`hashCode`, but with only one instance, equality is simply identity. Kotlin 1.9 made `data object`
stable, and it's the recommended form for the case of a sealed hierarchy that carries no data.

**Why the names are not HTTP names:** `SkuNotFound` rather than `NotFound404`. The repository
reports what it found in the database. The service turns that into a domain exception, and the
[handler](error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt.md) turns that into a status code.

## Check your understanding

- Why can't `removeStock` return `InventoryItem?` the way `addStock` does? What would the service be
  unable to tell apart?
- A teammate adds `data object SkuDiscontinued : PurchaseResult`. What happens when the project
  compiles, and where?
- Why is it `PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound` and not `PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound()`? What would
  `PurchaseResult.Purchased` without arguments mean?
- What would `println(PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock)` print with `data object`, and what would it print with a plain `object`?

trailing period, for the same reason as the `404` message: the id `CW-1.` is possible, and a period
after it would make the end of the id unclear.

repository's single statement doesn't return the current quantity on a refusal, and adding that

insufficient inventory". The handler follows the contract.

[SkuNotFoundException](SkuNotFoundException.kt.md#the-whole-class-in-one-line). Kotlin has no
checked exceptions, and a domain exception keeps HTTP status codes out of the service.

```kotlin

 * Returns [PurchaseResult.Purchased] with the remaining stock if successful, [PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock] if there is not enough quantity, [PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound] if the skuId doesn't exist.
 */

    // Why: One statement instead of two (update, then select), so another request can't change the stock between them (a race condition)
```

`InventoryItem?`. A purchase has three outcomes, and a `null` could only represent one of the two
failures. The result is always one of the three cases and is never `null`, so the type has no `?`.

declaration. When you hover the function in the editor, each one is clickable, and it jumps to that case.
It's Javadoc's `{@link PurchaseResult.Purchased}`, written more briefly. The precondition
"Quantity must be at least 1" is stated for the same reason as in `addStock`: nothing in this
function checks it. The [service's `require`](InventoryService.kt.md#purchaseinventory-one-branch-per-outcome)
does. For this function it matters even more. With `-5`, `quantity >= -5` is always true and
`quantity - (-5)` *adds* 5.

**Why one statement (Robert, 2026-09-29):** three designs were compared.

| Design | Round trips | Problem |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `UPDATE ... WHERE quantity >= ?`, and then, when it updates nothing, `SELECT` to find out why | 2 | Between the two statements the SKU can be created or restocked, so the reason the second query reports might not match what the `UPDATE` saw |
| A transaction with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, then decide in Kotlin, then `UPDATE` | 3 | Correct, but the row lock is held across three round trips *and* the Kotlin code in between |
| **One statement that updates and classifies (chosen)** | 1 | None: the check, the write and the classification happen together |

stock?" happens inside the `UPDATE`'s `WHERE` clause.

action `purchaseInventory`, the business word.

### The SQL: a data-modifying CTE

```kotlin
"""
    WITH purchased AS (
        UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - :requested_quantity
            WHERE sku_id = :skuId AND quantity >= :requested_quantity
                RETURNING quantity
    )

            EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM inventory WHERE sku_id = :skuId) AS sku_exists
"""
)
```

**SQL (`WITH ... AS (...)`, a CTE):** `WITH name AS (query)` defines a **common table expression**

similar to declaring a local `val` and then using it below. Here the CTE is an `UPDATE`, not a
`SELECT`. Postgres calls that a **data-modifying CTE**. The `UPDATE` runs exactly once, and its
`RETURNING` rows become the contents of `purchased`.

| Part | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `SET quantity = quantity - :requested_quantity` | subtract the requested amount |
| `WHERE sku_id = :skuId` | only this SKU (an exact, case-sensitive match) |
| `AND quantity >= :requested_quantity` | only if there's enough. `>=`, not `>`, so selling the last unit is allowed |
| `RETURNING quantity` | send back the new quantity; if no row was updated, send back nothing |

SQL were ever wrong.

line is Robert's layout. Postgres ignores it.

```kotlin
.param("skuId", skuId)

```

```kotlin
.query{rs, _ ->
```

| `NULL` | `false` | `SkuNotFound` |

because `remainingQuantity` is a local `val`: nothing can change it between the check and the use.
Java has no equivalent; you'd use the value and trust that the check was right.

**Kotlin (the lambda's value):** the lambda has two statements (`val`s) and then the `when`. As
with every lambda, the [last expression is the return value](#mapping-each-row-the-lambda), so
the `when`'s result, a `PurchaseResult`, is what the row mapper produces. The `when` is used as an
expression, not a statement, so each branch provides a value.

built from the function's `skuId` parameter. That's the same string, because the `WHERE` matched it
exactly.

the query and returns the one mapped row, and it throws if there are zero rows or more than one. Here
that can't happen, because the outer `SELECT` has no `FROM` and always returns exactly one row. That
guarantee is what makes `.single()` the correct choice here, where `addStock` needed
`.list().singleOrNull()`.

"""

| Part | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `SET quantity = quantity - :requested_quantity` | subtract the requested amount |

### `purchaseInventory`: one branch per outcome

```kotlin
/**
 * Removes quantity from a SKU's stock during a purchase. Returns the remaining InventoryItem on a success.
 * @throws SkuNotFoundException when no sku is found.
 * @throws InsufficientInventoryException if not enough quantity for the purchase.
 * @throws IllegalArgumentException if quantity is less than 1 (a caller bug, so it surfaces as a 500).
 */
fun purchaseInventory(skuId: String, quantity: Int): InventoryItem {
    // Why: @Valid only protects HTTP requests; this also stops direct callers (Can't have a 0 quantity in a purchase and a negative value would add stock.).
    require(quantity >= 1) {"quantity must be at least 1, was $quantity"}
    return when (val purchaseOutcome = inventoryRepository.removeStock(skuId,quantity)){
            is PurchaseResult.Purchased -> purchaseOutcome.item
            PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound -> throw SkuNotFoundException(skuId)
            PurchaseResult.InsufficientStock -> throw InsufficientInventoryException(skuId)
        }
}
```

**What it does:** it checks the argument, asks the repository to buy, and turns the repository's
[`PurchaseResult`](PurchaseResult.kt.md) into what the API needs. On success it returns the item;
for each failure it throws the matching domain exception.

**The `require`, again:** this is the same precondition as
[`receiveInventory`](#receiveinventory-a-precondition-and-a-block-body), and it matters more here.
With `-5`, the repository's `quantity >= -5` is always true and `quantity - (-5)` *adds* 5. The
database `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` wouldn't catch it, because the stock goes up, not down. Only this
line stops a purchase that adds stock. `InventoryServiceTest` checks `0` and `-5`.

**Kotlin (`when` with a subject):** `when (x) { ... }` compares one value, the **subject**, against
each branch in order. It's a much more capable version of Java's `switch`. The branches here use two
kinds of check:

| Branch | Kind | Means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `is PurchaseResult.Purchased ->` | type check | "is the subject a `Purchased`?" (Java's `instanceof`) |
| `PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound ->` | equality | "is the subject equal to the `SkuNotFound` object?" |

The two `data object`s have exactly one instance each, so an equality check is enough.
`is PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound` would also work. `Purchased` needs `is`, because every successful
purchase creates a new `Purchased`, and there's no single instance to compare against.

**Kotlin (`val` in the subject):** `when (val purchaseOutcome = ...)` calls the repository once,
names the result, and limits that name to the `when`. Outside the braces, `purchaseOutcome` doesn't
exist. The branches need the name, because `.item` is read from it.

**Kotlin (smart cast, with a type):** `purchaseOutcome` has the declared type `PurchaseResult`, and
that interface has no `item`. In the `is PurchaseResult.Purchased` branch, the compiler knows it's a
`Purchased`, so `purchaseOutcome.item` compiles. That's a
[smart cast](InventoryRepository.kt.md#choosing-the-outcome-a-when-without-a-subject), this time
from an `is` check instead of a null check. Think of `Purchased` as a box and `item` as what's inside
it: the service returns what's inside (`InventoryItem`), not the box. Java 16+ equivalent:

```java
if (outcome instanceof PurchaseResult.Purchased p) return p.item();
```

**Kotlin (exhaustive, with no `else`):** there are three branches and no `else`, and it compiles
because `PurchaseResult` is [sealed](PurchaseResult.kt.md#a-sealed-interface). The compiler knows
these are the only three cases, and it checks that each one is handled. That's better than adding an
`else`. If a fourth case were added to `PurchaseResult`, this `when` would stop compiling until
someone decided how the service handles it. With an `else`, the new case would silently fall into
whatever the `else` did.

**Kotlin (`when` is an expression):** the `when` produces a value, and `return` returns it. The
branches have the types `InventoryItem`, `Nothing` and `Nothing`
([`throw` is an expression of type `Nothing`](#getinventory-turning-no-row-into-an-error)), so the
whole `when` has type `InventoryItem`, which matches the return type. The same `Nothing` rule is
what lets `?: throw` produce a non-null result in `getInventory`.

**Watch out: `return` and a line break.** `return` and the start of the `when` have to be on the
same line. In Kotlin, a line break after a bare `return` ends the statement, so this:

```kotlin
return
    when (val purchaseOutcome = ...) { ... }
```

is parsed as `return` with no value, followed by an unreachable `when`. The compiler rejects it,
because the function has to return an `InventoryItem`. Robert ran into this while writing the
function. Java doesn't have this trap, because semicolons, not line breaks, end statements.

**Why the exceptions are thrown here:** the repository reports *what happened*, and the service
decides *what that means*. This follows the same split as
[`getInventory`](#getinventory-turning-no-row-into-an-error). `SkuNotFoundException` is the same
exception `GET /inventory/{skuId}` uses, so the purchase endpoint's `404` comes from the same
handler with the same body.

**KDoc:** one `@throws` for each exception a caller can see, each saying *when*. "Returns the
remaining InventoryItem" says what the `200` body contains: the stock after the purchase, not the
amount bought. Robert changed it from "the new InventoryItem" in review, to match the controller's
KDoc and the contract's "remaining inventory for the SKU".

**Naming:** `purchaseInventory` is the business word. The repository's `removeStock` is the data
word for the same action, the same pairing as `receiveInventory` and `addStock`.

**Kotlin:** `removeStock(skuId,quantity)` with no space after the comma, and `){` with no space,
are both legal.

The two `data object`s have exactly one instance each, so an equality check is enough.
`is PurchaseResult.SkuNotFound` would also work. `Purchased` needs `is`, because every successful
purchase creates a new `Purchased`, and there's no single instance to compare against.

**Kotlin (`val` in the subject):** `when (val purchaseOutcome = ...)` calls the repository once,
names the result, and limits that name to the `when`. Outside the braces, `purchaseOutcome` doesn't
exist. The branches need the name, because `.item` is read from it.

**Kotlin (smart cast, with a type):** `purchaseOutcome` has the declared type `PurchaseResult`, and
that interface has no `item`. In the `is PurchaseResult.Purchased` branch, the compiler knows it's a
`Purchased`, so `purchaseOutcome.item` compiles. That's a
[smart cast](InventoryRepository.kt.md#choosing-the-outcome-a-when-without-a-subject), this time
from an `is` check instead of a null check. Think of `Purchased` as a box and `item` as what's inside
it: the service returns what's inside (`InventoryItem`), not the box. Java 16+ equivalent:

```java
if (outcome instanceof PurchaseResult.Purchased p) return p.item();
```

**Kotlin (exhaustive, with no `else`):** there are three branches and no `else`, and it compiles
because `PurchaseResult` is [sealed](PurchaseResult.kt.md#a-sealed-interface). The compiler knows
these are the only three cases, and it checks that each one is handled. That's better than adding an
`else`. If a fourth case were added to `PurchaseResult`, this `when` would stop compiling until
someone decided how the service handles it. With an `else`, the new case would silently fall into
whatever the `else` did.

**Kotlin (`when` is an expression):** the `when` produces a value, and `return` returns it. The
branches have the types `InventoryItem`, `Nothing` and `Nothing`
([`throw` is an expression of type `Nothing`](#getinventory-turning-no-row-into-an-error)), so the
whole `when` has type `InventoryItem`, which matches the return type. The same `Nothing` rule is
what lets `?: throw` produce a non-null result in `getInventory`.

**Watch out: `return` and a line break.** `return` and the start of the `when` have to be on the
same line. In Kotlin, a line break after a bare `return` ends the statement, so this:

```kotlin
return
    when (val purchaseOutcome = ...) { ... }
```

is parsed as `return` with no value, followed by an unreachable `when`. The compiler rejects it,
because the function has to return an `InventoryItem`. Robert ran into this while writing the
function. Java doesn't have this trap, because semicolons, not line breaks, end statements.

**Why the exceptions are thrown here:** the repository reports *what happened*, and the service
decides *what that means*. This follows the same split as
[`getInventory`](#getinventory-turning-no-row-into-an-error). `SkuNotFoundException` is the same
exception `GET /inventory/{skuId}` uses, so the purchase endpoint's `404` comes from the same
handler with the same body.

**KDoc:** one `@throws` for each exception a caller can see, each saying *when*. "Returns the
remaining InventoryItem" says what the `200` body contains: the stock after the purchase, not the
amount bought. Robert changed it from "the new InventoryItem" in review, to match the controller's
KDoc and the contract's "remaining inventory for the SKU".

**Naming:** `purchaseInventory` is the business word. The repository's `removeStock` is the data
word for the same action, the same pairing as `receiveInventory` and `addStock`.

**Kotlin:** `removeStock(skuId,quantity)` with no space after the comma, and `){` with no space,
are both legal.

### The fourth `// Contract:` comment

```kotlin
// Contract: paths./inventory/{skuId}/purchase.post - 200 application/json with InventoryItem, 400 text/plain for a quantity below 1, an unreadable body, the wrong Content-Type, or insufficient amount of inventory, 404 text/plain for SKU not found.
```

**Contract:** `paths./inventory/{skuId}/purchase.post` (`operationId: purchaseItem`) lists three
responses: `200` with an `InventoryItem` ("remaining inventory for the item"), `400` "Insufficient
inventory or invalid request", and `404` "SKU not found", both as `text/plain`. The contract names
only one `400` case, insufficient inventory. The three invalid-request cases are the same README
"Contract gaps" decisions as for `POST /inventory/{skuId}`, because the request body is the same
`InventoryQuantity`. Like the comments above it, this one lists outcomes that other files produce,
so a reader knows which handlers to look for.

### `POST /inventory/{skuId}/purchase`

```kotlin
/**
 * Removes quantity from the SKU's stock on a purchase, and returns the remaining stock for POST /inventory/{skuId}/purchase.
 */
@PostMapping("/{skuId}/purchase")
fun purchaseInventory(@PathVariable skuId: String, @Valid @RequestBody requestQuantity: InventoryQuantity): InventoryItem = inventoryService.purchaseInventory(skuId, requestQuantity.quantity)
```

**Spring (a path with a fixed segment):** `"/{skuId}/purchase"` has two segments. `{skuId}` matches
any text, and `purchase` matches only that exact word. Added to the class's `/inventory`, it gives
`/inventory/{skuId}/purchase`. Spring now has three mappings on paths below `/inventory/`:

| Request | Mapping | Function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /inventory/widget` | `GET /{skuId}` | `getInventory` |
| `POST /inventory/widget` | `POST /{skuId}` | `receiveInventory` |
| `POST /inventory/widget/purchase` | `POST /{skuId}/purchase` | `purchaseInventory` |
| `GET /inventory/widget/purchase` | the path matches, the method doesn't | Spring answers `405 Method Not Allowed` |

A path variable matches exactly one segment, so `/{skuId}` never matches `widget/purchase`. The
reverse case is worth knowing: `POST /inventory/purchase` is a *receive* for a SKU called
`purchase`, because `purchase` there sits in the `{skuId}` position. The contract doesn't forbid that
id, and the routing handles it correctly.

**Spring (the same body handling as receive):** `@Valid @RequestBody requestQuantity: InventoryQuantity`
is the same parameter as in [`receiveInventory`](#post-inventoryskuid), because the contract uses the same
`InventoryQuantity` schema for both endpoints. The same four steps run in the same order, and only the
last one differs:

| Step | Fails when | Handler's response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Find a converter for the `Content-Type` | not JSON | `400 Content-Type must be application/json` |
| 2. Jackson reads the body | empty, malformed, wrong type, `null`, too big | `400 Invalid request body` |
| 3. `@Valid` runs Bean Validation | `quantity < 1` | `400 quantity must be at least 1` |
| 4. The function calls the service | no such SKU | `404 SKU not found: <skuId>` |
| | not enough stock | `400 Insufficient inventory for <skuId>` |

No new handler was needed for steps 1 to 3: the [exception handler](error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt.md)
is global, so the handlers written for receive also cover purchase. Step 4 reuses the `404` handler
from `GET /inventory/{skuId}` and adds one new handler for insufficient stock.

**Why an invalid body on a missing SKU is a `400` (Robert, 2026-09-29):** `POST /inventory/missing/purchase`
with `{"quantity": 0}` has two problems. Steps 1 to 3 run before this function, and the database is
only asked about the SKU in step 4, so the client gets the `400`. That's Spring's natural order, and
it's also the cheaper one: a request with a bad body never reaches the database. The alternative
(check the SKU first, and return `404`) would mean reading the path variable and querying the
database before validating the body. `InventoryControllerTest` pins the order.

**Kotlin:** an expression body that passes `requestQuantity.quantity` to the service, not the object,
the same as [receive](#post-inventoryskuid). The service never depends on a web class.

**Why `200`:** the contract lists `200` for a successful purchase, and returning `InventoryItem` gives
Spring's default `200`. The body is the stock *after* the purchase (the repository's `RETURNING`
row), which is why the KDoc says "returns the remaining stock". Robert changed "new" to "remaining"
in review.

**Naming:** `purchaseInventory` matches the service function (the "one name through the layers"
rule), not the contract's `operationId: purchaseItem`. The same trade-off was made for
`receiveInventory` and `createInventory`.

**KDoc:** written as a multi-line `/** ... */` with the text on its own line. That's the same KDoc as
the one-line form, formatted differently.

| `POST /inventory/widget` | `POST /{skuId}` | `receiveInventory` |
| `POST /inventory/widget/purchase` | `POST /{skuId}/purchase` | `purchaseInventory` |
| `GET /inventory/widget/purchase` | the path matches, the method doesn't | Spring answers `405 Method Not Allowed` |

A path variable matches exactly one segment, so `/{skuId}` never matches `widget/purchase`. The
reverse case is worth knowing: `POST /inventory/purchase` is a *receive* for a SKU called
`purchase`, because `purchase` there sits in the `{skuId}` position. The contract doesn't forbid that
id, and the routing handles it correctly.

**Spring (the same body handling as receive):** `@Valid @RequestBody requestQuantity: InventoryQuantity`
is the same parameter as in [`receiveInventory`](#post-inventoryskuid), because the contract uses the same
`InventoryQuantity` schema for both endpoints. The same four steps run in the same order, and only the
last one differs:

| Step | Fails when | Handler's response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Find a converter for the `Content-Type` | not JSON | `400 Content-Type must be application/json` |
| 2. Jackson reads the body | empty, malformed, wrong type, `null`, too big | `400 Invalid request body` |
| 3. `@Valid` runs Bean Validation | `quantity < 1` | `400 quantity must be at least 1` |
| 4. The function calls the service | no such SKU | `404 SKU not found: <skuId>` |
| | not enough stock | `400 Insufficient inventory for <skuId>` |

No new handler was needed for steps 1 to 3: the [exception handler](error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt.md)
is global, so the handlers written for receive also cover purchase. Step 4 reuses the `404` handler
from `GET /inventory/{skuId}` and adds one new handler for insufficient stock.

**Why an invalid body on a missing SKU is a `400` (Robert, 2026-09-29):** `POST /inventory/missing/purchase`
with `{"quantity": 0}` has two problems. Steps 1 to 3 run before this function, and the database is
only asked about the SKU in step 4, so the client gets the `400`. That's Spring's natural order, and
it's also the cheaper one: a request with a bad body never reaches the database. The alternative
(check the SKU first, and return `404`) would mean reading the path variable and querying the
database before validating the body. `InventoryControllerTest` pins the order.

**Kotlin:** an expression body that passes `requestQuantity.quantity` to the service, not the object,
the same as [receive](#post-inventoryskuid). The service never depends on a web class.

**Why `200`:** the contract lists `200` for a successful purchase, and returning `InventoryItem` gives
Spring's default `200`. The body is the stock *after* the purchase (the repository's `RETURNING`
row), which is why the KDoc says "returns the remaining stock". Robert changed "new" to "remaining"
in review.

**Naming:** `purchaseInventory` matches the service function (the "one name through the layers"
rule), not the contract's `operationId: purchaseItem`. The same trade-off was made for
`receiveInventory` and `createInventory`.

**KDoc:** written as a multi-line `/** ... */` with the text on its own line. That's the same KDoc as
the one-line form, formatted differently.

### `handleInsufficientInventory`: the exception comes in as a parameter

```kotlin
// Contract: paths./inventory/{skuId}/purchase.post - when there is insufficient inventory for a purchase call we return 400 text/plain.

/** Returns a 400 text/plain response with the message from the exception: Insufficient inventory for <skuId> */
@ExceptionHandler(InsufficientInventoryException::class)
fun handleInsufficientInventory(ex: InsufficientInventoryException): ResponseEntity<String> =

    ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST)
        .contentType(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
        .body(ex.message ?: "Insufficient Inventory")
```

**Spring:** the same shape as [`handleStockOverflow`](#handlestockoverflow-our-exception-our-message):
our own exception, a `400`, and our own message as the body. The body is
`Insufficient inventory for <skuId>`, written in
[InsufficientInventoryException](InsufficientInventoryException.kt.md).

**Spring (why `ex` must be declared):** this handler reads the exception, so it needs a parameter
to receive it. [`handleInvalidRequestBody`](#handleinvalidrequestbody-a-handler-with-no-parameters)
shows the opposite case. There the body is fixed text, so the parameter can be left out. Here the
body includes the SKU, so the handler needs the exception object. Spring decides what to pass by
the parameter's **type**: it sees `ex: InsufficientInventoryException` and passes in the exception
that was thrown. The name `ex` is only a convention and has no special meaning. `e` or `error` would
work just as well.

Robert's versions show the two mistakes to avoid (2026-09-29):
1. **A fixed body, `"Insufficient Inventory"`.** It compiles, but the controller test expects
   `Insufficient inventory for widget`, and the fixed text loses the SKU.
2. **`.body(ex.message ...)` with `()` still empty.** `ex` was never declared in this function, so
   the compiler reports `Unresolved reference 'ex'`. `ex` in the other handlers is each one's
   own parameter. A parameter name exists only inside the function that declares it, as in Java,
   where `void handle(InsufficientInventoryException ex)` is the only way to get an `ex`.

**Kotlin (the fallback):** as in the other handlers, `?:` is there only because `Throwable.message`
is `String?`. The constructor always sets a message, so the fallback never runs. Its capitalization,
`Inventory`, differs from the real message's `inventory`. That's harmless, because it's unreachable.

**Contract:** `paths./inventory/{skuId}/purchase.post`, response `'400'`, `text/plain`. The
contract's own description names this case: "Insufficient inventory or invalid request".
`InventoryControllerTest` checks the status, the content type and the exact body.

content.content:
(`check_violation`). Spring translates that error into a `DataIntegrityViolationException`.

The purchase `UPDATE` will already refuse to oversell through its `WHERE quantity >= ?`, so this
constraint only matters if application code has a bug. That's the point of a second line of
defense. The test `database rejects an update that would make quantity negative` in
`InventoryRepositoryTest` deliberately runs an unguarded `UPDATE` to prove it.
---

**Why `null` and not an exception here:** "no row" is a normal answer to a database question,
not an error. Turning it into "404 SKU not found" is a business decision, so it belongs in the
service. That keeps the repository reusable: purchase will look SKUs up too, and it treats a
missing one differently from low stock.

### Zero stock is found
---
for overflow), so a nullable type is enough. A purchase has three: purchased, SKU not found, and
not enough stock. `null` can't say *which* failure happened, and the API needs a `404` for one and
a `400` for the other. `PurchaseResult` is a sealed type with one case per outcome (Robert's
[PurchaseResult.kt](../../main/inventory/PurchaseResult.kt.md) explains it once he's written it).

---
`ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ...)` would carry the status itself, which puts HTTP
into the service. A custom exception keeps HTTP out of it: the service says *what* went wrong, and the handler decides how
that looks over HTTP. The purchase endpoint will throw the same exception for a missing SKU, and
the same handler will map it. (`ResponseStatusException` also doesn't give a `text/plain` body by
default; see [the handler notes](InventoryExceptionHandler.kt.md#the-class-and-why-its-an-advice).)

lines: -# SkuNotFoundException.kt

-> Source: [src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/error/SkuNotFoundException.kt](../../../../../../src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/error/SkuNotFoundException.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-27
-## Role
-The project's first custom exception, written by Robert. It names a domain problem, "this SKU
-doesn't exist", without saying anything about HTTP. The [service](../InventoryService.kt.md) throws
-it when the [repository](../InventoryRepository.kt.md) finds no row. It passes through the
-[controller](../InventoryController.kt.md) untouched, and
-[InventoryExceptionHandler](InventoryExceptionHandler.kt.md) turns it into a `404` with a
-`text/plain` body.
-It lives in the `error` subpackage, which was Robert's proposal (2026-09-27): custom exceptions and
-the handler that maps them sit together, apart from the controller → service → repository files.
-The alternatives were a flat `inventory` package (the error types mixed in with the layers) and a
-top-level `com.robertwoolbright.inventory.error` (shared by every feature, but this project has only one).
-## Walkthrough
-### The package
-```kotlin
-package com.robertwoolbright.inventory.inventory.error
-**Kotlin:** the package matches the folder `inventory/error/`. The compiler doesn't require that,
-but the Kotlin style guide recommends it (Java tooling expects it), and every file in this project
-follows it. Code in the
-parent `inventory` package must import this class, as the [service does](../InventoryService.kt.md#imports).
-### The whole class in one line
-```kotlin
-/** Thrown when the database is queried with the SKU, but the result comes back as null. This is thrown at the service level and is mapped to a 404 by InventoryExceptionHandler. */
-class SkuNotFoundException(skuId: String) : RuntimeException("SKU not found: $skuId")
-**Kotlin (extending a class):** `: RuntimeException(...)` after the constructor means "extends
-`RuntimeException`". It's Java's `extends RuntimeException` plus a `super(...)` call in one step. The
-parentheses are the call to the superclass constructor, and they're required: Kotlin always makes you
-say which superclass constructor runs. Java equivalent:
-```java
-public class SkuNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {
-    public SkuNotFoundException(String skuId) {
-        super("SKU not found: " + skuId);
-**Kotlin (a plain constructor parameter):** `skuId: String` has no `val` or `var`, so it is *only* a
-constructor parameter, not a property. It can be used while the object is being built (here, in the
-superclass call), and then it's gone. `exception.skuId` doesn't compile. Compare
-[`private val` in the repository](../InventoryRepository.kt.md#a-spring-bean-with-constructor-injection),
-which keeps the value as a field. The SKU survives only inside the message text, which is all the
-handler needs.
-**Kotlin (storage vs visibility, two separate settings):** `private val` combines two keywords that
-answer different questions. They are easy to mix up (the 2026-09-28 walkthrough first tried
-`private` to make `ex.skuId` reachable, which does the opposite):
-| Setting | Keyword | Question it answers |
-| Storage | `val` / `var` | Is the value kept on the object after the constructor runs? |
-| Visibility | `private` / none (public) | Who can read it once it's kept? |
-```kotlin
-class SkuNotFoundException(skuId: String)              // not stored      → ex.skuId: compile error
-class SkuNotFoundException(val skuId: String)          // stored, public  → ex.skuId works anywhere
-class SkuNotFoundException(private val skuId: String)  // stored, private → only inside this class
-class SkuNotFoundException(private skuId: String)      // doesn't compile: nothing is stored to hide
-So the one-word change that makes `ex.skuId` compile in the handler is `val`. The layers use
-`private val` for the opposite reason: each one stores its dependency, and hides it so the layer above
-can't skip past it. `inventoryService.inventoryRepository.findBySkuId(...)` from the controller

lines: -# Kotlin & Spring Concepts Index
-A running index of every Kotlin and Spring concept used in this codebase. Each row links to
-the study notes that explain it in full (see [notes/README.md](notes/README.md)). `/sync-docs`
-and `/walkthrough` add rows as new concepts come up.
-## Kotlin
-| Concept | What it is | First seen |

-| Component scanning and stereotypes | `@Repository`/`@Service`/`@RestController` make scanned classes beans; `@Import` registers one by hand | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md) |

-| The service layer | Business rules and error mapping sit between HTTP (controller) and SQL (repository) | [InventoryService.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryService.kt.md) |

-| Singleton beans and threads | One bean instance, built at startup, serves every request thread at once, so beans must be stateless | [InventoryController.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryController.kt.md) |
-| Named parameters in SQL | `:skuId` + `.param("skuId", value)` binds the value separately, preventing SQL injection | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md) |

-| `@PathVariable` and path templates | `@GetMapping("/{skuId}")` matches one path segment and binds it to the same-named parameter | [InventoryController.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryController.kt.md) |

-| Domain exceptions | The service throws a domain error (`SkuNotFoundException`); a handler decides the HTTP status | [SkuNotFoundException.kt](notes/main/inventory/error/SkuNotFoundException.kt.md) |

-| `@RestControllerAdvice` + `@ExceptionHandler` | One class that catches exceptions from every controller; within a class the closest exception type wins, across advice classes their `@Order` decides first | [InventoryExceptionHandler.kt](notes/main/inventory/error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt.md) |

-| Exception resolver chain | Spring catches every controller exception: `@ExceptionHandler` (controller, then advice) → `@ResponseStatus` → built-in mappings → `500` | [InventoryExceptionHandler.kt](notes/main/inventory/error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt.md) |

-| When mistakes surface | Compile time (types), startup (missing beans), first request (strings: paths, SQL, missing advice); only request-level tests catch the last | [InventoryController.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryController.kt.md) |

-| `ResponseEntity` builder | `status(...).contentType(...).body(...)` sets status, headers and body; `notFound()` has no body | [InventoryExceptionHandler.kt](notes/main/inventory/error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt.md) |
-| `@ParameterizedTest` + `@ValueSource` | One test method run once per supplied value, each reported separately | [InventoryControllerTest.kt](notes/test/inventory/InventoryControllerTest.kt.md) |

-| Test transactions are per thread | A `@JdbcTest` rollback covers only the test thread; worker threads commit on their own connections | [InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt](notes/test/inventory/InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt.md) |
-| Start gate (`CountDownLatch`) | Hold N threads at one line, then release them together so they really overlap | [InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt](notes/test/inventory/InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt.md) |
-| `@PostMapping` + `@RequestBody` | Map a POST; Jackson reads the JSON body into a class through its primary constructor | [InventoryController.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryController.kt.md) |

-| `@Valid` + Bean Validation (`@Min`) | Constraints on a request class run only when the parameter has `@Valid`; failures throw `MethodArgumentNotValidException` | [InventoryQuantity.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryQuantity.kt.md) |

-| Request body failure order | Content-Type → JSON read → validation → the function; each failure is its own Spring exception | [InventoryController.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryController.kt.md) |

-| Handling Spring's own exceptions | Advice handlers run before Spring's built-in resolver, so they can replace its `415`/empty `400`; never send Spring's `ex.message` to clients | [InventoryExceptionHandler.kt](notes/main/inventory/error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt.md) |

-| `@ExceptionHandler` with no parameter | The annotation routes the exception; the parameter is only needed to read it | [InventoryExceptionHandler.kt](notes/main/inventory/error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt.md) |
-| Three layers of checks | `@Valid` for clients (400), `require` for our own callers (500), DB `CHECK` as the backstop | [InventoryService.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryService.kt.md) |

-| Default response status | A plain return value is `200`; `201` needs `@ResponseStatus` or a `ResponseEntity`. Defaults are invisible in code, so tests pin them | [InventoryController.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryController.kt.md#post-inventoryskuid) |
-## Database and API design
-| Concept | What it is | First seen |

-| Contract schemas are not tables | OpenAPI schemas describe JSON on the wire; tables describe what's stored | [V1__create_inventory.sql](notes/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md) |
-| Natural vs surrogate key | `sku_id` as the primary key vs a generated `id` plus a unique `sku_id` | [V1__create_inventory.sql](notes/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md) |

-| Constraints as a backstop | `PRIMARY KEY`, `NOT NULL`, `CHECK` protect data even when app code is wrong | [V1__create_inventory.sql](notes/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md) |

-| Identifier case folding | Postgres lowercases unquoted names; use `snake_case` in SQL, `camelCase` in Kotlin | [V1__create_inventory.sql](notes/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md) |
-| Upsert and `EXCLUDED` | `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`; `EXCLUDED` is the row the insert tried to add | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md#the-upsert) |
-| `RETURNING` | A write returns the changed row in the same statement; no second `SELECT` | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md#the-upsert) |

-| Lost update (find-then-write race) | Two requests read the same value and the second write erases the first; one atomic statement prevents it | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md#addstock-the-signature-and-the-two-decisions) |

-| Overflow-safe guard | `current <= MAX - new` instead of `current + new <= MAX`, which itself overflows | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md#the-overflow-guard) |

+| Implicit lambda parameter `it` | A one-parameter lambda can leave the parameter out and use `it` | [InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt](notes/test/inventory/InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt.md) |

+| Block body vs expression body | `= expr` holds one expression; two steps (check, then act) read better as `{ }` with an explicit `return` | [InventoryService.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryService.kt.md) |
+| Class with no constructor parameters | `class E : RuntimeException("msg")`, created with `E()` | [AddStockOverflowException.kt](notes/main/inventory/error/AddStockOverflowException.kt.md) |

+| Sealed interfaces | `sealed interface` closes the list of implementations (same package + module), so a `when` over it can be exhaustive; Java 17's `sealed ... permits` | [PurchaseResult.kt](notes/main/inventory/PurchaseResult.kt.md) |

+## Spring
+| Concept | What it is | First seen |
+| `@SpringBootApplication` | `@Configuration` + `@EnableAutoConfiguration` + `@ComponentScan` from this package down | [InventoryApplication.kt](notes/main/InventoryApplication.kt.md) |
+| Starters and the Boot BOM | Starters bundle dependencies; the dependency-management plugin supplies versions | [build.gradle.kts](notes/build.gradle.kts.md) |
+| Docker Compose support | `bootRun` starts compose.yaml and wires the DataSource | [compose.yaml](notes/compose.yaml.md) |

+| Property source precedence | Command line > environment variables > application.yml > defaults; relaxed binding maps `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` to `spring.datasource.url` | [application.yml](notes/main/resources/application.yml.md) |

+| YAML map properties | `spring.jackson.deserialization:` binds its children into a `Map<Feature, Boolean>`; each indent level is one segment of the dotted name | [application.yml](notes/main/resources/application.yml.md#strict-json-the-jackson-block) |

+| Strict JSON (Jackson 3) | `accept-float-as-int` / `allow-coercion-of-scalars` off, so `1.5` and `"5"` are 400s instead of guesses; a non-null `Int` rejects `{}` and `null` | [application.yml](notes/main/resources/application.yml.md#strict-json-the-jackson-block) |
+| Bean Validation starter | `spring-boot-starter-validation`: `jakarta.validation` annotations + Hibernate Validator, run on `@Valid @RequestBody` | [build.gradle.kts](notes/build.gradle.kts.md) |
+| Connection details | Compose / Testcontainers supply the DB connection, overriding `spring.datasource.*` | [application.yml](notes/main/resources/application.yml.md) |
+| Test context caching | Identical test configurations share one context (and container) until the run ends | [TestcontainersConfiguration.kt](notes/test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md) |
+| `@TestConfiguration` + `@Import` | Test-only beans that component scanning skips | [TestcontainersConfiguration.kt](notes/test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md) |
+| `@ServiceConnection` | A Testcontainers container supplies DataSource connection details | [TestcontainersConfiguration.kt](notes/test/support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md) |
+| `@SpringBootTest` | Starts the full application context in a test | [InventoryApplicationTests.kt](notes/test/InventoryApplicationTests.kt.md) |
+| Exception translation | SQL errors become `DataAccessException`s, e.g. `DataIntegrityViolationException` | [InventoryRepositoryTest.kt](notes/test/inventory/InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md) |
+| `@JdbcTest` slice | JDBC-only context, no component scan, each test rolled back | [InventoryRepositoryTest.kt](notes/test/inventory/InventoryRepositoryTest.kt.md) |
+| `@AutoConfigureMockMvc` + Kotlin MockMvc DSL | In-process HTTP requests; `mockMvc.get(...).andExpect { }` | [InventoryControllerTest.kt](notes/test/inventory/InventoryControllerTest.kt.md) |
+| `JsonCompareMode.STRICT` | Exact JSON match: no extra fields, array order matters | [InventoryControllerTest.kt](notes/test/inventory/InventoryControllerTest.kt.md) |

+| Flyway migrations | `V<n>__<desc>.sql` (two underscores) in `db/migration`, run once at startup, checksummed; wrong names are skipped silently | [V1__create_inventory.sql](notes/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md) |

+| Migrations are changes, not snapshots | A schema change is a new `V2__` with `ALTER TABLE`; the schema is the whole V1→Vn chain | [V1__create_inventory.sql](notes/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md) |

+| Component scanning and stereotypes | `@Repository`/`@Service`/`@RestController` make scanned classes beans; `@Import` registers one by hand | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md) |
+| Constructor injection | A single constructor is autowired without `@Autowired`; beans are created at startup | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md) |
+| `JdbcClient` query chain | `sql(...)` prepares, `query { row mapper }` maps, `list()` runs and collects | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md) |

+| `@RestController` vs `@Controller` | `@RestController` = `@Controller` + `@ResponseBody`: return values are written as the body, not rendered as views | [InventoryController.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryController.kt.md) |
+| `@RequestMapping` + `@GetMapping` | Class-level base path plus method-level mappings; the function name doesn't matter | [InventoryController.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryController.kt.md) |
+| Message converters (Jackson) | A `@ResponseBody` value is written as JSON; Kotlin property names become JSON keys | [InventoryController.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryController.kt.md) |
+| The service layer | Business rules and error mapping sit between HTTP (controller) and SQL (repository) | [InventoryService.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryService.kt.md) |

+| Singleton beans and threads | One bean instance, built at startup, serves every request thread at once, so beans must be stateless | [InventoryController.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryController.kt.md) |
+| Named parameters in SQL | `:skuId` + `.param("skuId", value)` binds the value separately, preventing SQL injection | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md) |

+| `@PathVariable` and path templates | `@GetMapping("/{skuId}")` matches one path segment and binds it to the same-named parameter | [InventoryController.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryController.kt.md) |

+| `@ParameterizedTest` + `@ValueSource` | One test method run once per supplied value, each reported separately | [InventoryControllerTest.kt](notes/test/inventory/InventoryControllerTest.kt.md) |
+| `@RepeatedTest` | Runs a test N times; used for intermittent concurrency bugs | [InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt](notes/test/inventory/InventoryConcurrencyTest.kt.md) |

+| `@ExceptionHandler` with no parameter | The annotation routes the exception; the parameter is only needed to read it | [InventoryExceptionHandler.kt](notes/main/inventory/error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt.md) |
+| Three layers of checks | `@Valid` for clients (400), `require` for our own callers (500), DB `CHECK` as the backstop | [InventoryService.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryService.kt.md) |

+| Default response status | A plain return value is `200`; `201` needs `@ResponseStatus` or a `ResponseEntity`. Defaults are invisible in code, so tests pin them | [InventoryController.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryController.kt.md#post-inventoryskuid) |

+## Database and API design
+| Concept | What it is | First seen |

+| Contract schemas are not tables | OpenAPI schemas describe JSON on the wire; tables describe what's stored | [V1__create_inventory.sql](notes/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md) |
+| Natural vs surrogate key | `sku_id` as the primary key vs a generated `id` plus a unique `sku_id` | [V1__create_inventory.sql](notes/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md) |

+| Constraints as a backstop | `PRIMARY KEY`, `NOT NULL`, `CHECK` protect data even when app code is wrong | [V1__create_inventory.sql](notes/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md) |

+| Identifier case folding | Postgres lowercases unquoted names; use `snake_case` in SQL, `camelCase` in Kotlin | [V1__create_inventory.sql](notes/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md) |
+| Upsert and `EXCLUDED` | `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`; `EXCLUDED` is the row the insert tried to add | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md#the-upsert) |
+| `RETURNING` | A write returns the changed row in the same statement; no second `SELECT` | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md#the-upsert) |

+| Lost update (find-then-write race) | Two requests read the same value and the second write erases the first; one atomic statement prevents it | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md#addstock-the-signature-and-the-two-decisions) |

+| Overflow-safe guard | `current <= MAX - new` instead of `current + new <= MAX`, which itself overflows | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md#the-overflow-guard) |

+| Data-modifying CTE | `WITH x AS (UPDATE ... RETURNING ...) SELECT ...`: a write and a read in one atomic statement | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md#the-sql-a-data-modifying-cte) |

+| One snapshot per statement | Every part of a statement sees the data as it was when it started; only `RETURNING` shows the CTE's change | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md#the-sql-a-data-modifying-cte) |

+| Scalar subquery, `EXISTS`, `SELECT 1` | `(SELECT ...)` as a value is `NULL` for no rows; `EXISTS` is `true`/`false`, never `NULL` | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md#the-sql-a-data-modifying-cte) |

+| Conditional `UPDATE` under concurrency | Under `READ COMMITTED`, a waiting `UPDATE` re-checks its `WHERE` on the committed row, so two buyers can't both take the last unit | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md#the-sql-a-data-modifying-cte) |

+| JDBC `NULL` vs `0` | `getInt` returns `0` for `NULL`; `getObject(col, Int::class.javaObjectType)` keeps `null` | [InventoryRepository.kt](notes/main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md#reading-the-row-null-is-not-0) |

## Project layout

```text
build.gradle.kts         The build: plugins, dependencies, Kotlin/Java settings
settings.gradle.kts      Project name (single-module build)
gradlew, gradle/wrapper/ Gradle wrapper; pins the Gradle version, nothing to install
compose.yaml             Local Postgres for bootRun
src/main/
  kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/
    InventoryApplication.kt   Entry point; component scan starts here
    inventory/                The inventory feature: controller, service, repository, models
      error/                  Domain exceptions and the handler that maps them to HTTP errors
  resources/
    application.yml           Spring Boot configuration
    db/migration/             Flyway SQL migrations (V1__..., V2__...)
    openapi/inventory.yaml    The OpenAPI contract (source of truth)
src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/
  inventory/                  Feature tests: repository, service, controller, concurrency races
  support/                    Shared test setup (the Testcontainers Postgres)
.claude/                 Claude Code configuration (hooks, agents, skills) — see below
CLAUDE.md                Project memory and coding standards for Claude Code
docs/
  learning/
    notes/               Study notes: one per source file, explaining it chunk by chunk
    walkthroughs/        Logs of each /walkthrough session
    kotlin-concepts.md   Index of every Kotlin/Spring concept, linked to its notes
  ai-sessions/           Exported transcripts of every AI session on this project
scripts/                 Hook scripts (branch guard, KDoc check, session export)
```

**Package by feature.** Code is grouped by what it does (`inventory/`), not by technical
layer (`controller/`, `service/`, `repository/`). File names still show the layer, so the
controller → service → repository flow is easy to follow. This is a general JVM/Spring
convention, not a Kotlin rule. One Kotlin difference is worth knowing: Kotlin has no
package-private visibility. Its `internal` modifier means "visible within this Gradle
module", so package boundaries are organizational, not enforced by the compiler.
